This rumor was quickly picked up and circulated by online gaming circles, gaining steam due to growing uncertainty around the game’s status.

It has been revealed that marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra was revealed in 2022 and stars Captain America and Black Panther (Azurri, T'Challa's grandfather), alongside Howling Commandos member Gabriel Jones and Wakandan Spy Network leader Nanali, as they battle Hydra during World War II. Developed by Skydance New Media, led by Amy Hennig, it’s been repeatedly delayed, and only cinematic footage has been released. This has understandably caused many to question the game’s fate.

However, a few hours after the cancellation rumor made the rounds, Bloomberg’s Jason Schreier reported on Bluesky that Skydance’s leadership addressed the rumor with the development team on Slack and assured them Marvel 1943 was not canceled. However, Schreier adds this could change due to the uncertainty caused by the recent merger between Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount Skydance (Skydance New Media is a game development branch of the now-merged Skydance Corporation).

Skydance Games told the development team behind Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra on Slack this afternoon that the game is not canceled, despite a widely circulated rumor on Twitter today claiming that it was.

Furthermore, Kotaku’s Rebekah Valentine clarified in her report that Marvel 1943 executive producer Lu Giglotti told staff in a Skydance Slack message he’d spoken directly with the executive leadership team to confirm Marvel 1943 is still alive, saying, "There is no truth to these claims." According to Kotaku’s report, Giglotti informed the team that Marvel 1943 was approaching an Alpha milestone later this month. Giglotti also told staff not to let the rumor distract them and that Skydance was "monitoring the situation" to address in the future.

Kotaku’s report also sheds light on the game’s tumultuous development cycle. Marvel 1943 was originally pitched as a Netflix game before it was eventually turned into a console and PC title. This transition means the current iteration is “light on gameplay” and lacks substantial interactions, with players primarily using a single button to play it.

Recent findings suggest that this isn't a completely surprising revelation, as Marvel 1943 was billed as a narrative-driven, linear single-player experience when it was revealed, but the style of game has never been clear. The same reveal also saw Skydance promise the game boasted "intuitive controls and exhilarating second-to-second gameplay that captures the action and excitement of Marvel, inspired by landmark comics, television, and films, as they navigate this all-newly introduced globe-trotting adventure." This disconnect may be attributed to Kotaku also reporting that Marvel 1943 is “well over budget,” and its overall scope has been heavily scaled back. Regardless, the outlet’s source claims the game is “close to done.”.

Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra was initially slated to launch in 2025. It was then delayed to early 2026 "to add more polish", according to Skydance, before being pushed again to an undetermined launch window. The game has no announced platforms.

It has been revealed that although Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra appears safe for now, other recent projects have not been as fortunate. Be sure to read our stories about the recent high-profile cancellations of Gang of Dragon and Fairgames.

[Sources: Jason Schreier, Kotaku].

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, the game has been gaining momentum since the launch of a demo in October last year, but the developer never quite managed to commit to a date for its debut title.
  • In a recent development, seed Sparkle Lab confirmed today that Starsand Island will enter Early Access on February 11, which is only a bit over one week from now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, though it may seem like we just had a significant life sim release in Heartopia, 2026 actually has more than one highly-anticipated release in that particular subgenre of cozy game. The next big one on the horizon is Starsand Island, the life and farming sim from Seed Sparkle Lab.

In a recent development, the game has been gaining momentum since the launch of a demo in October last year, but the developer never quite managed to commit to a date for its debut title. Until now.

In a recent development, seed Sparkle Lab confirmed today that Starsand Island will enter Early Access on February 11, which is only a bit over one week from now. This goes for Steam and the Xbox Preview Program version.

The developer remarked to expect a fairly short Early Access run, as the full launch is expected in the summer of this year. When the full release arrives, the game will also make the jump to PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series, as well as Switch 2.

The full release is also expected to bring Steam Deck support and introduce the multiplayer mode, which will not be available during Early Access.

Sources indicate that starsand Island has something of a unique look compared to other games in the subgenre. The storybook, anime-inspired aesthetics are popular in the realm of gacha games, of course. However, seeing as this particular game isn’t gacha, being a premium product means it’s going to offer something free-to-play games aren’t designed to.

According to recent reports, speaking of which, the game will be available in two editions: Standard and Deluxe, with the latter including Romanticism-inspired outfits, furniture, and other customisation items. If you buy either during launch, you’ll also get a Chinese Fresh Year bonus with even more outfits and furniture.

On top of the usual systems of farming, mining, and making friends with adorable characters (and animals), the game also has combat that pits you against ancient guardians. You can, of course, also build a home in it, and decorate it to your heart's content.

Seed Sparkle Lab states you can expect about 100 hours of content in the Early Access launch build, and more features will arrive over the course of the next six or so months, including a crossover event with My Time At Portia.

You can look forward to more Starsand Island coverage from us in the near future. Until then, you can get started by planning who you’re going to date now.

8 Things You Must Do Before Ending Chapter One in GTA 6

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1139 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There is a lot that you can do in the first chapter of Grand Theft Auto 6.
  • After chapter one, everything in GTA 6 changes, and you don’t have the opportunity to get everything done that you might want to, so you want to be sure that you have a checklist and that you complete it before making your way to Vice City and starting bigger and better things.
  • Recent findings suggest that note: It is crucial to note that taking up Mattia’s offer will end the first chapter of the game.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is a lot that you can do in the first chapter of Grand Theft Auto 6. You can deep sea dive for treasure, hang out with friends, complete missions, set up for Lucia, and a lot more. However, some of this absolutely needs to be done before you hit the end of the first chapter.

After chapter one, everything in GTA 6 changes, and you don’t have the opportunity to get everything done that you might want to, so you want to be sure that you have a checklist and that you complete it before making your way to Vice City and starting bigger and better things.

Recent findings suggest that note: It is crucial to note that taking up Mattia’s offer will end the first chapter of the game. There will also be spoilers ahead about chapter one.

Recent findings suggest that jason and Lucia have a chance to be madly in love in the beginning of the game. If you prepare for Lucia to get out of prison, work on Jason’s appearance, and focus on how they interact with each other, it will build a solid foundation.

It has been revealed that there is a hard reset that comes at the end of the first chapter, and for a while, Lucia will be on her own while Jason recovers. With that being said, it will take a bit of a toll on their relationship.

This means that if you raise it up very high in the beginning, you won’t need to worry about needing to rebuild it as much later in the game, saving you a bit of time later on.

Immediately after setting up your BuckMe account, you are told that you need to start saving money. The first goal in the game is to have a total savings of $5,000 stashed away. This is a pretty easy goal to hit, especially since there are a fair number of money-making opportunities in the first chapter.

You want to make sure that you hit this goal, as when the hard reset comes at the end of the chapter, you will lose everything except what is in your savings account.

As an added bonus, putting money away into your savings account will also raise your relationship, so it is a win-win situation. After you have everything saved up, the rest of your money is stuff you can play with.

Now that you have saved up the necessary cash for your family savings account, you might have some money burning a hole in your pocket. It is time to go on a bit of a shopping spree.

As I noted, you won’t be able to take this money with you into chapter two, so you will want to spend all of it. Buy some clothes, and definitely upgrade your weapons.

There is no point in upgrading your car, as you will lose this after chapter one. Instead, focus on increasing your wardrobe and upgrading your weapons as these will carry over into the next chapter.

In a recent development, there are some missions that you only have access to in the first chapter, and some of them belong to Shirley - Jason’s neighbor. She is a kind lady, and she will occasionally ask you to complete a few tasks.

These consist of getting her some alcohol, and stealing a mobility scooter from a lady nearby. They are fun short missions that you can complete within a few minutes, but they are worth doing because they are quite fun.

Sources indicate that don’t worry about the treasure hunting, as you will be able to come back to it later on. Only certain missions disappear after the first chapter.

There’s tons of details in GTA 6, which means that there are a bunch of collectibles that you can find scattered about. Some of these collectibles are books and magazines, and several of them are found around Jason’s house.

Before you end chapter one, you will want to get the books around Jason’s house. These include one in the bedroom, two in the living room, a magazine on the back deck, and one in the shed. Each of these disappears after the first chapter.

It has been revealed that along with this, you will want to grab the sunglasses in Donny’s trailer. You will make your way over there during one of the missions in the first chapter, so you shouldn’t miss out on them, but make sure to pick them up while you have the chance.

If you have been focused on upgrading your weapons, gathering clothes, and putting money into your savings, then you will probably need some extra cash in the first chapter. Instead of searching for treasure, you should instead focus on completing the lost drug missions.

In a recent development, there are four lost drug missions around Key Lento and up to the Grassrivers. These are special missions that end up disappearing after chapter one ends, so you will not have the ability to go back and complete them later on.

Since this is the only time you have access to them, you may as well complete them for the extra cash and spend it on stuff that will help you later in the game.

It has been revealed that while I have already established that buying weapons is important because they carry over, it is also important to grab the unique weapons that are obtainable early in the game. There are a couple weapons that you can find around the islands in Key Lento, and they will carry you in later parts of the game.

For instance, the Assassin Pistol can be found on a small dinghy on an island and it is great for completing missions stealthily in later parts of the game, and it has become one of my go-to weapons for staying hidden.

There is also a shotgun that you can find that is quite powerful. It gets outclassed by other unique weapons later on, but it is great to have in chapter two.

Recent findings suggest that one thing that is nice about GTA 6 is that it gives you the option to manually save. This means that you can create save points at key points in the game so that you can return to them later on.

I highly recommend completing what you can in chapter one and then creating a save point right before you go to do the tourist trap mission, as this is the last mission of the chapter, and it is also the point of no return.

If you want to play the game over but don’t want to deal with the slower pacing of the first chapter, you can skip all of that with a save right before the chapter change.

Industry observers note that it sounds like Koei Tecmo’s decision to finally release a Nioh game on PC day-and-date with PlayStation has paid off. The highly-anticipated Nioh 3 has gone live across both platforms, a first for a series that typically spends its initial release months as a console exclusive.

On Steam, and despite having only been available for just a few hours, the game has broken series records, and it continues to climb.

At the time of writing, Nioh 3 has peaked at 42,822 concurrent players on Steam (via SteamDB), and the number keeps going up. Because it’s in the middle of day in Europe and everyone is at work, it’s entirely possible - if not likely - that this figure will get much higher. A weekend bump is also possible, as we’ve seen with several recent releases.

As it stands, the current peak concurrent is enough to get the game in Steam’s top 20 most played games.

This already puts it ahead of all other Nioh games on Steam. The original Nioh peaked at 10,649 when it released in November, 2017. Nioh 2 fared much better, peaking at 41,325 concurrent players in February, 2021.

According to recent reports, of course, you could see that success coming a mile away. The game is right now number one worldwide in Steam’s list of top sellers. This is a jump of 46 positions, for a total of three weeks Nioh 3 has spent in that list.

There are many reasons as to why Nioh 3 has done as well as it has. Word of mouth coming off last year’s PS5-exclusive demo, and the more positive coverage that followed since are just two.

Just last week, Team Ninja released a pretty generous demo across both platforms, which has been well received by players, and likely contributed to sales, in no small part because progress in the demo carries over to the full game.

Sources indicate that critical reviews have been incredibly positive, too. We awarded the game four out of five stars, calling it “Team Ninja’s most accomplished action game, and the series’ most accessible.” It will be interesting to see what number the highest peak concurrent actually settles on over the weekend.

Until then, if you’re jumping in yourself, our Nioh 3 guides are essential reading. Start off with these useful and actually informative gameplay tips, and don’t start playing until you’ve changed these settings. Once you’re ready to get deeper, be sure to read up on how to play co-op with other players, and how to summon AI Acolytes to help you out.

#224192. Scientists discover a hidden gut defense that could prevent colon cancer

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1818 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists discover a hidden gut defense that could prevent colon cancer

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1818 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A common antibody found throughout the digestive tract may provide an unexpected defense against colon cancer.
  • It has been revealed that in a study published in Nature, scientists found that mice missing a type of antibody known as immunoglobulin A (IgA) developed more than twice as many colon tumors as mice with normal levels of the antibody.
  • Even more promising, when the team administered IgA orally to mice that lacked the antibody, the animals no longer indicated an elevated risk of developing tumors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A common antibody found throughout the digestive tract may provide an unexpected defense against colon cancer. Researchers at Rockefeller University have discovered that these immune molecules help regulate the growth of cells lining the intestine, potentially preventing the uncontrolled cell division that can lead to tumors.

It has been revealed that in a study published in Nature, scientists found that mice missing a type of antibody known as immunoglobulin A (IgA) developed more than twice as many colon tumors as mice with normal levels of the antibody. The researchers also uncovered how this protection works. IgA attaches to cells along the intestinal lining and helps prevent them from multiplying too rapidly.

Even more promising, when the team administered IgA orally to mice that lacked the antibody, the animals no longer indicated an elevated risk of developing tumors.

According to recent reports, "One intriguing aspect of this work is that it highlights how a natural defense in the gut restrains the cell division that can lead to cancer," indicates senior author Daniel Mucida, who leads Rockefeller's Laboratory of Mucosal Immunology. "Most cancer research focuses on trying to destroy a tumor that already exists, but what if we could intervene before tumors form?".

The findings may help explain why people with IgA deficiency, a condition in which the body produces little or none of this antibody, face a greater risk of colorectal cancer. They also offer new insight into how gut bacteria, immune defenses, and intestinal cells work together to influence cancer development, potentially even in people with otherwise healthy immune systems.

Why the Gut Contains So Much of This Antibody.

IgA is one of the immune system's most abundant antibodies in the digestive tract, where it provides an important early defense against potentially harmful microbes. Unlike antibodies that recognize a single specific target, IgA can interact with many different kinds of gut bacteria and even certain healthy cells belonging to the body.

According to recent reports, scientists have known for decades that the intestines contain unusually large quantities of IgA. However, the reasons for its abundance, and the full range of functions it performs, have remained incompletely understood.

Industry observers note that mucida's laboratory investigates how the intestine manages two essential but sometimes competing responsibilities. It must defend the body against dangerous microorganisms while allowing nutrients from food to pass into the bloodstream. Earlier research from his team has also helped explain how immune cells in the digestive tract contribute to food intolerances and allergies.

For the new study, Gregory Donaldson, a former postdoctoral researcher at Rockefeller who is now an assistant professor at UCLA, set out to better understand how IgA interacts with intestinal bacteria and whether those interactions might influence the development of colon cancer.

According to recent reports, "We know these antibodies bind bacteria and, by doing so, can shape the microbiome," he claims. "And because IgA deficiency, which affects about 1 in 500 people in the U.S., is linked to colorectal cancer, I wondered whether these interactions might be relevant to the disease.".

It has been revealed that the microbiome is the community of microorganisms living in and on the body. In the intestines, these microbes perform key functions related to digestion and immune health, but certain bacteria can also contribute to disease under the wrong conditions.

Missing Gut Antibodies More Than Doubled Colon Tumors.

To investigate IgA's protective effects, Donaldson compared mice that could not produce the antibody with mice that had normal IgA levels. Both groups were raised together, allowing the researchers to control for differences in food and exposure to microorganisms.

The results revealed a striking difference. Animals without IgA developed substantially more colorectal tumors than their counterparts, consistent with the increased colorectal cancer risk observed in humans with IgA deficiency.

The association was not limited to a single experimental setup. Researchers observed the same pattern using multiple models of colon cancer, strengthening the evidence that IgA plays a meaningful protective role.

"We found this was true for several different kinds of models of colon cancer, so that was a really convincing effect," notes Donaldson.

Sources indicate that the team then tested whether replacing the missing antibody could reverse the effect. When mice lacking IgA received oral doses of the antibody, their increased susceptibility to colon tumors disappeared.

According to recent reports, this result suggested that IgA does more than simply accompany other protective processes in the intestine. Its presence appears to directly influence conditions that determine whether tumors develop.

Scientists Discover a Natural Brake on Cancer Cell Growth.

It has been revealed that to understand the mechanism behind this protection, the researchers examined epithelial cells, which form the inner lining of the intestine. These cells are particularly important because colon cancer begins when cells in this tissue undergo changes that allow them to grow uncontrollably.

It has been revealed that the intestinal lining is constantly renewing itself. Older or damaged cells are replaced by newly introduced ones, making controlled cell division essential for keeping the digestive tract healthy. However, when the signals that regulate this process become disrupted, excessive growth can create opportunities for cancer to develop.

Industry observers note that in mice without IgA, the researchers identified changes in gene activity associated with cell proliferation, the process through which cells divide and increase in number. Crucially, these changes appeared before any tumors became visible, suggesting that the antibody helps regulate an early step in cancer development.

"We assumed there must be some sort of receptor on the epithelial cells that was mediating this," Donaldson states.

The researchers suspected that IgA was interacting with a specific molecular structure on the surface of intestinal cells, allowing it to influence how those cells behaved.

Gabriella Lima dos Reis, the study's second author and a graduate student working in Gabriel Victora's laboratory, investigated a promising candidate called DMBT1.

DMBT1 is a receptor found on the surface of epithelial cells that can bind to IgA. Previous research had connected it to several types of cancer, but scientists had not established precisely how it functions in the development of colon tumors.

How Gut Bacteria and IgA Control Tumor Formation.

Further experiments revealed that DMBT1 plays two very different roles depending on whether IgA is present.

According to recent reports, when intestinal bacteria are present, DMBT1 activates signals that encourage epithelial cells to divide. This response is part of the normal activity of the intestinal lining, which must continually replace cells to maintain its protective barrier.

Sources indicate that igA helps keep that growth under control. When the antibody binds to DMBT1, it restrains the receptor's activity, effectively acting as a brake on cell proliferation.

Without IgA, however, DMBT1 signaling can continue without sufficient restraint. Intestinal cells then divide more rapidly than they should, increasing the likelihood that tumors will develop.

In a recent development, the researchers confirmed that this excessive growth depends on several interacting factors. When gut bacteria were absent, DMBT1 signaling was disabled, or normal amounts of IgA were available, epithelial cell division remained under control.

Together, these findings reveal how a common immune molecule helps maintain the delicate balance between necessary tissue renewal and potentially dangerous overgrowth.

It has been revealed that "If IgA is missing, epithelial cells that are performing their normal function -- responding to bacteria by producing newly introduced cells -- can keep dividing unchecked, leading to cancer," Mucida states. "We think this homeostatic effect is IgA's main function. This was a substantial surprise.".

According to recent reports, homeostasis refers to the body's ability to maintain stable, healthy conditions despite constant changes in its environment. In this case, IgA appears to support that balance by preventing normal intestinal cell renewal from becoming excessive.

A Upcoming Possibility for Preventing Colon Cancer.

By identifying DMBT1's normal role in intestinal cells, the Rockefeller team has uncovered a potential target for future colon cancer prevention strategies.

Instead of waiting until a tumor develops and then attempting to destroy it, researchers may eventually be able to influence the biological signals that make tumors more likely to form.

"Based on the mechanism we discovered, perhaps we could influence epithelial cells to be less likely to develop into a tumor," Mucida says. "We know, for example, that having polyps increases your chances of getting colon cancer, so we think that there could be an opportunity to target this pathway after polyps are removed. Right now, there are no interventions available at that point.".

Colon polyps are growths that develop along the inner lining of the large intestine. Although many are harmless, some can eventually become cancerous. Removing them during a colonoscopy can reduce cancer risk, but researchers are interested in finding additional ways to prevent future tumors from developing.

The newly identified IgA and DMBT1 pathway could offer one such opportunity, although additional research is needed to determine whether targeting it would be effective and safe in humans.

Could Beneficial Gut Bacteria Help Prevent Cancer?

The discovery also raises another intriguing possibility. Certain intestinal bacteria may actively help protect against cancer by influencing how epithelial cells behave or by encouraging the production of protective antibodies.

While much of the research into the gut microbiome and cancer has focused on harmful bacteria that promote tumor formation or accelerate cancer growth, some microbes may have the opposite effect.

"What is potentially even more exciting is that there is evidence that individual species of bacteria can have really specific effects on epithelial cells as well," Donaldson notes. "A lot of research has focused on bacteria that induce tumors or can exacerbate their growth, but we have some evidence that there are bacteria that could do the opposite, just as IgA does. To that end, perhaps we could develop a probiotic supplement that induces a protective IgA response. This is all very speculative, but it's one direction that we could look towards in the future.".

Recent findings suggest that such an approach would aim to use beneficial microorganisms to stimulate the body's existing protective mechanisms rather than directly attacking cancer cells. However, the idea remains speculative, and the mouse experiments do not establish that taking IgA supplements or probiotics can prevent colon cancer in people.

For now, the findings provide a clearer picture of how the immune system and gut microbiome cooperate to maintain healthy intestinal tissue. They also suggest that some of the body's most notable defenses against cancer may operate long before the disease becomes detectable.

Mucida adds, "Overall, there is a lot more to learn about how the dance between bacteria, antibodies, and epithelial cells in the gut works to maintain health.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that hoYoverse just wrapped up a big Honkai: Star Rail Special Program. We’ve been waiting for this one for a couple of weeks now thanks to a delay, but the developer has finally delivered all the news on Version 4.0, which will arrive February 13.

According to recent reports, the upcoming major release is dubbed No Aha at Full Moon for a very good reason. Aha's Planarcadia is the big latest world headlining Version 4.0.

Planarcadia is a place whose description sounds a bit like a Warhammer 40,000 Eldar homeworld, and is quite open about its cyberpunk inspirations. In-universe, however, it was born out of the pages of an art canvas, and it’s a world where pleasure is king.

The squad’s host in this chapter is Madam Pearl, who will oversee the the Astral Express’ return to the place where they first began their journey. Duomension City is where you’re going to land, and meet the creatures that dwell in this world.

The imagenae of Planarcadia require attention to survive, and they feed off people’s Wishpower. If they don’t get any attention, they perish, which does tie into the general themes of the place. Duomension City has other interesting locations that you’re going to visit, such as the Graphia Academy art school, the commercial district of Dovebrook, and a few other places hidden behind mysterious entrances.

It has been revealed that the Phantasmoon Games is another highlight of Planarcadia, a competitive spectacle where you’ll have a chance to compete to become Aeon for a Minute. If you make it to the final stages, you may earn an audience with The Laughter.

Much like the world where the games take place, the whole point of the competition is to attract the most attention, so rules are a bit loose as to how you manage to do that. The event will bring together several of the game’s factions, though not everyone is there for the competition.

Industry observers note that as you explore Planarcadia, if you have characters on your team who are on the newly-playable Path of Elation, you’ll earn Punchlines. The more you accumulate, the closer you get to catching Aha’s attention, which triggers Aha Instant.

Industry observers note that version 4.0 introduces two new 5-Star characters to Honkai: Star Rail. General Yao Guang (Madam Yao) is one, a Seer Strategist from the Xianzhou Alliance's Yuque. If you’ve been playing the game, you may already be familiar with her voice, as she's previously been in touch with our heroes via radio link. But V4.0 marks her first on-screen appearance, as well as her playable debut.

General Yao Guang is a Physical character on the Path of Elation whose specialty is using Weal and Woe Lots in battle, which she uses to increase Elation for allies, and grant everyone Punchline any time she uses a Skill. If an Aha Instant is triggered, she casts Woe Lots, which debuff enemies, causing them to take increased damage, all while regenerating Skill Points for the rest of the team.

Industry observers note that her aptly named Certified Banger buff adds one extra instance of Elation to teammates’ attacks. And her Ultimate grants the team Punchline, and triggers an extra Aha Instant.

The other newly introduced arrival is likewise a Path of Elation devotee. Sparxie is a suspiciously familiar streamer who uses her influencer skills in combat. When she fights, she turns the fight into a battle for attention, as she forces enemies to engage in a race for upvotes.

Industry observers note that when you consume Skill Points, Sparxie will get gifts, which in turn cause her to regenerate Skill Points and Punchlines for the team. You can continue doing this to increase your damage. When Aha Instant is triggered, Sparxie unleashes a lucky draw that deals damage to enemies with each bounce.

She also benefits from the Certified Banger state, which causes the gifs she receives to deal more Elation damage to a random enemy target. Her Ultimate also deals more Elation damage.

Industry observers note that version 4.0 will see a few re-runs, too. Black Swan, Evernight, and Hysilens will be part of the first half's Warp events. The second half will see the return of Sparkle, Cerydra, and Rappa — that's right, HoYoverse have finally remembered Rappa exists, after one of the longest rerun waits in the game's history! Both Black Swan and Sparkle are getting a few tweaks to their kit with this version, too, so the timing works.

Finally, the other major news is a Fortnite collaboration. Starting February 26, Kafka and Blade will join Epic’s battle royale shooter. On that day, you’ll find skins of the two Stellaron Hunters in the Fortnite Item Shop, and the new outfits are even compatible with Fortnite's LEGO styles. You can also expect other customisation bits like Back Bling, Pickaxe, and more to be part of the package.

Sources indicate that if you download the game on the Epic Games Store, and take part in Honkai: Star Rail-themed activities, you’ll also get the Blade character outfit in Fortnite for free. Event schedule and timing will be announced at a later date.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's been less than a week since Grand Theft Auto 6 came out, and Rockstar Games has already found another way to get us to spend money on the game. If you've been collecting sports cards while exploring Leonida, you'll soon be able to do the same outside the game. Rockstar has partnered with Panini America to bring these fictional sports trading cards to life, and they'll be out in December 2026.

This goes beyond your usual video game merchandise featuring the main characters. The cards are based on collectibles that actually exist within GTA 6's world, so you might recognize some of the athletes and teams when you open a pack. And if you're hoping to get your hands on some of the rarer cards, there are even a few that are limited to a single copy each.

According to recent reports, panini America declared its partnership with Rockstar Games on November 24. The officially licensed set is called the GTA VI: Sports Trading Card Collection, and it'll be the first trading card collaboration between the two companies.

Industry observers note that if you've ever collected football or basketball cards, chances are you're already familiar with Panini. They're also known for reprinting comics in Europe, and I still have a copy of the X-Men: The Last Stand Annual 2007 published by Panini Books.

In a recent development, what's different this time is that instead of collecting cards featuring actual sports stars, you'll be collecting ones based on athletes from Rockstar's fictional universe. The promotional artwork shows a mixture of illustrated cards and ones featuring character renders, much like those found in the game itself.

In a recent development, the cards will come in boxes containing four packs each. Panini says a box will typically include two Rookie cards, a Retro card, an Illustrated card and four Special Silvers. These are average figures rather than guaranteed contents for every box.

There'll also be different colored variants of the cards, including silver, pink, teal and light blue, along with team-colored parallels. The rarest variants have much smaller print runs. The Legend Bronze cards are numbered out of 49, the numbered Silver variants out of 25, and the Gold variants are one-of-a-kind cards.

Considering how many people are playing GTA 6 right now, I wouldn’t be surprised if some of the rare cards ended up selling for ridiculous prices.

Getting your hands on every variant, however, could be quite a challenge. Considering how many people are playing GTA 6 right now, I wouldn't be surprised if some of the rarer cards ended up selling for ridiculous prices.

Even if you don't care about the numbered cards, there's some appeal in having the regular ones. GTA's fictional athletes aren't exactly household names like the ones you'd find in Panini's other sports collections, but you can actually go looking for their cards in Leonida while playing the game.

Rockstar has been selling GTA merchandise for years, but this particular collaboration reminds me of the sort of extras that used to come with physical copies of video games. The maps that came with older GTA titles, for instance, were something you could actually use while playing and keep long after you were done with the game.

In a recent development, ironically, GTA 6's boxed edition doesn't even come with a game disc. So it's nice to see Rockstar making something physical that draws directly from the game rather than simply putting its logo on another piece of merchandise.

According to recent reports, rockstar could've easily gone with a conventional trading card set featuring Jason, Lucia, and other major characters. Instead, it's making replicas of things you might stumble across while taking a break from the story. I'd love to see Rockstar do something similar with other fictional brands from the series, like Sprunk or eCola.

Unfortunately, Panini hasn't announced an exact release date, pricing, or which countries the cards will be available in.

Depending on when the cards go on sale in December, they could make for a pretty good Christmas gift for a GTA fan.

Breaking: Tested: 1979 Buick Century Turbo Coupe Is a Rolling Contradiction

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2349 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Caranddriver

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A paradox, according to a well­-thumbed copy of Webster’s Fresh World, is a statement that seems contradictory, but may be true.
  • On the other hand we have this Tur­bo Coupe posturing about in its rackish, spoilered finery, squatting on its we­-mean-business fat tires, its twin pipes burbling, acting more Trans Am than Buick.
  • Industry observers note that buick started making out-of-character performance noises a few years ago when its chief engineer, Lloyd Reuss, and a band of enthusiastic young engi­neers decided to crank up a turbocharg­ing project for the V-6 engine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the June 1979 issue of Car and Driver.

Recent findings suggest that A paradox, according to a well­-thumbed copy of Webster’s Fresh World, is a statement that seems contradictory, but may be true. Which brings us imme­diately to the Buick Century Turbo Coupe. On one hand it most definitely is a Buick, which is automatically a state­ment. As most of us were growing up, the Buicks in our lives belonged to the family doctor or other such community pillars. Buicks were sedate, relatively ex­pensive cars—stop-offs on the way up the GM ladder for the man with the growing bank account, or the highest reasonable aspirations for the workaday man who longed to rise out of Ford and Chevy land.

On the other hand we have this Tur­bo Coupe posturing about in its rackish, spoilered finery, squatting on its we­-mean-business fat tires, its twin pipes burbling, acting more Trans Am than Buick. A contradiction.

Industry observers note that buick started making out-of-character performance noises a few years ago when its chief engineer, Lloyd Reuss, and a band of enthusiastic young engi­neers decided to crank up a turbocharg­ing project for the V-6 engine. Their ef­forts were first seen in the 1975 Indy pace car, which also sported some very un-Buick-like suspension. In 1977 Buick offered a slick Sport Coupe variation on the LeSabre and Regal theme. The Le­Sabre version we tested was so good it elicited comments like “a breath of fresh air for people who’ve hungered to own a good-handling American car.” And one exuberant staffer said all it needed was a three-pointed star on the hood to make it a Mercedes-class piece. In 1978 the turbo motor went into pro­duction, and the stage was set for this year's Turbo Coupe.

See all results for used cars for sale near 07104.

Sources indicate that bruce Robinson is a project engineer at Buick’s Flint, Michigan, headquar­ters, and one of those enthusiastic types Reuss brought in to spice up Buick’s slide-rule department. Reuss is gone now—he’s chief engineer over at Chev­rolet—but Robinson and the Reuss en­thusiasm still exist. Robinson was as­signed the Turbo Coupe. He didn’t build it single-handedly, but as much as any car that pops off the line can be remarked to be one man’s baby, the Turbo Coupe is his.

“We wanted to go from GT, like the LeSabre and Regal Sport Coupes, to All Out,” Robinson explains. “We wanted to make it go, and handle, and stop like no other Buick.”.

Sources indicate that he did it, he explains, by creating what Buick now calls the FE1 package, a giant step up from the existing FE2, which is Buick’s equivalent of Chevro­let’s famous F41 handling upgrade. The FE1, available only on the Turbo Coupe, is basically stiffer springs, steer­ing changes, and wider wheels. The front spring rates have been increased from the regular Sport Coupe specs of 365 pounds per inch to a giganto 440. Rear springs are up to 140 lbs/in from 125. (For further comparison, the base V-6 Century coupe has spring rates, front/rear, of 300/115.) Anti-roll bars are the same for FE1 and FE2: 32 mm front, 22 mm rear; but another big up­grade for the Turbo came in the rear upper-control-arm bushings, little de­vices we don’t think much about but which have a lot to do with transient re­sponse. The base and Sport Coupe ver­sions have bushings rated at 20,000 lbs/in; the Turbo Coupe is fitted with 35,000-lbs/in bushings. Rounding out the FE2 package is a quicker steering ra­tio, 14:1 instead of 15.13:1, and P205/70R-14 radials on seven-inch rims.

See all results for used cars for sale near 07104.

But as much as we wanted to know all that good spring and tire stuff, we were even more curious about the exhaust system. It is, in a word, loud. We spent a lot of time playing with the throttle and letting off in low and second just to hear that sound-from-the-past, that Golden Oldie exhaust noise. How'd Robinson do it?

Sources indicate that the sound, he reveals, was a specifi­cally planned part of the overall image. They got it by the simple expedient of routing the exhaust into a single con­verter and then out into a pair of ex­haust pipes that carry a resonator each. No mufflers.

“A delightful byproduct,” Robinson gleefully reveals, “was an extra ten horsepower due to the reduced back pressure.” The odds on finding ten horsepower these days without spend­ing ’leventeen trillion dollars in devel­opment are about the same as Bianca and her pals dropping by your place for dinner tonight: slim to none.

According to recent reports, that throaty exhaust note, by the way, is more evident inside the Turbo Coupe than outside. The body acts as a sound chamber to increase the effect. “The noise level passed the EPA tests,” Robinson notes, “but we’re not about to ask them to check it again to make sure.” Right.

It has been revealed that so Robinson and his associates have built a Buick with all the right suspen­sion bits and pieces, they’ve come up with a creditable 175 horses to move it around, they’ve given it an exhaust sys­tem to warm the cockles of an old hot rodder’s heart, and they’ve dressed it up with spoilers and flat-black paint. Why, we had to wonder, after doing all that, did they leave out some traditional, mandatory even, performance-car parts, like a manual transmission and an in­strument panel with some gauges?

Sources indicate that “Simple,” Robinson claims. “Money.”.

Adding a manual transmission would have required a complete 50,000-mile EPA durability test, and that costs hun­dreds of thousands. Ditto a different in­strument panel. Buick didn’t have any­thing on the shelf that would have bolt­ed in. Designing a new panel and tool­ing up to produce it would also have cost hundreds of thousands.

It has been revealed that “Anything you spend on building a new model, or a new version of an exist­ing car,” Robinson explains, “you have to figure you can recover in sales.” And Buick doesn’t figure to sell too many Turbo Coupes, it turns out. It's an image car, a showroom-traffic build­er, so if you see one on the floor of your local Buick dealer, you’re probably looking at his allotment for the year. Should you jump at it?

According to recent reports, the Turbo Coupe is easily the best-­looking of all the “aero” designs, which Buick and Olds offer in two- and four­-door versions. The improvement in looks seems to come from the simple addition of the rear-deck spoiler, which also happens to reduce overall drag, Buick reports, by a healthy 18 percent. (The two-door aero design, by the way, will be around at least through 1980; the ugly four-door is going away.).

It has been revealed that inside, as we’ve hinted, there is little to distinguish the Turbo Coupe from its lesser brethren. The handsome, but un­informative, instrument panel contains a tricolor turbo-boost indicator that reads out in one, A Little, and Whoosh. Our test car had vinyl buckets, and while they provide pretty good sup­port in all the right places, they are as slick as greased owl potty. Cloth is avail­able, however, and we recommend it.

Over the road, the Turbo’s yes-I-am, no-I’m-not nature surfaces again. De­spite all the good things Robinson and his merry band have wrought, the car’s manners are still rather Buick-like. Which isn’t necessarily all bad. Your teeth aren’t jarred by every tar strip, and the car is very quiet at cruise. But there is an unexpected numbness in the steering that should have been factored out. Response is good, but that all-important feel is missing.

Despite the suspension modifications, the Turbo Coupe is still an understeer­er. That’s to be expected, so no points lost there. General Motors is a firm be­liever that understeer is safer than over­steer. Better, the reasoning goes, the in­competents plow off the road nose-first, scrubbing speed all the way, than have the tail leading the procession at prodi­gious speed. Fair enough, because the knowledgeable Trans Am or Z28 driver can put the boot into his mount at the proper time and induce some very pleasant oversteer. Not so with the Tur­bo Coupe; the little engine-that-would­-be-a-V-8 just doesn’t produce enough torque quickly enough to let you play the tail-out game with much success. The boost gauge may be up there in Whoosh, but the tail will be dutifully following the furrow the front end is plowing. We’re talking about out there at the cop-baiting, wife-scaring, dog­-cowering limit, of course. In normal brisk motoring, the suspension does a good job. There’s no willow-wallow here, thank you.

The Coupe also does other good things. You’ll note that our comparison graphs show it at the top in acceleration ­and braking. Straight-line numbers will not disappoint.

According to recent reports, the Turbo Coupe certainly has the flash and dash Buick wants for its show­rooms, and it’s sure to draw its share of peekers and pokers and hood lifters. The traditional Buick buyer will peek and poke and then head off to the Elec­tra or LeSabre four-doors. The curious that stopped off on their way to price Trans Am and Z28s will poke and peek with a good bit more interest. And when they learn they can have a bare-bones Turbo Coupe for a little more than $6000, they may even give it some seri­ous thought. But our best guess is they’ll eventually find their way back to those other showrooms. The Turbo Coupe, as good a Buick as it is, doesn’t seem to be right for either group.

Industry observers note that what we want is Bruce Robinson and his boys to turn their attention to a latest Skylark Sport Coupe. Turbo that little honey, slap the FE1 package on it, and stand back. When we suggested that to Robinson, his eyes lit up with what could only be engineer-type lust. So maybe it’ll happen. And maybe it’ll even have a tachometer.

I must admit, the first night I drove the Turbo Coupe I kept putting my foot into it and running up through the gears, then backing off and doing it again and again, all the way home. The pumped-up little six, all snarling and willing, was just too inviting for me to ignore. Sometimes I’d even drop it into low and back off just to listen to the popping of the exhaust as it simmered down. I acted as silly as a newly licensed adolescent that night, but you just can’t resist playing in the Turbo Coupe. It’s that kind of car.

But what turned me on the most was the message hidden within its sophisticat­ed mechanicals: a fresh generation of mus­cle cars, one that pays its respects to both ecology and our tight petroleum supply, is not only possible, it’s just around the corner. All Buick has to do is work its tur­bocharging wizardry on the half-ton-­lighter Skylark front-driver and we’ll have the first of that new breed. Let us pray. —Rich Ceppos.

It has been revealed that I happen to be a firm believer in turbo­charging and all the wonderful things it can do for our cars—David E. Davis, Jr., to the contrary—but this Turbo Coupe from Buick stretches the very heartstrings of my enthusiasm. Past the limit. It’s a horrible fate for any engine as spunky as Buick’s turbo V-6. This motor should be zapping around a 2000-pound sports car or burning the tires off Buick’s chic little Skyhawk. Instead, it’s sentenced to the homeliest hunchback sedan Buick has stamped out in recent history. Grown men wince at the sight of this TR7 garage on wheels. And I wince at the thought of such an eager engine straining its heart out against a 3500-pound curb weight and an automatic transmission, without so much as a tachometer or a boost gauge to register the effort. To finish off the in­sult, this Century’s all gussied up in what I assume is Buick’s idea of a performance disguise. It looks like something the local sheriff would use to sneak up on the kids down at Shakey's. They wouldn’t be con­vinced, and neither am I. —Don Sherman.

Normally, when you dip the accelerator on a six-cylinder American car, it gives you the feeling you’re saving gas. Saving gas is a noble pastime but the feeling of saving gas is drudgery, right up there with Cometing out the sink.

That is why I think this Buick stands to give the American six-cylinder a good name. When you dip the pedal, things hap­pen. First off, the whole dashboard glows orange. (Knepper said the illumination comes from the boost light, but it’s hidden behind so many spokes and switches that I never actually saw it.) Then the exhaust turns mean and the bucket seat gets all pushy. Instead of saving gas, you get the feeling you’re hurrying.

Really, except for a count of the spark-­plug wires, there’s nothing six-cylinder about this car. It feels more like a high schooler’s hot rod, glass packs and all, and I had the urge to head on down to the drive-in and burn some rubber. I haven’t been in that mood for years. —Patrick Bedard.

Scientists discover a fresh type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (961 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly identified form of depression may help explain why some people struggle to find relief from commonly prescribed antidepressants.
  • Sources indicate that the discovery emerged from an analysis of clinical and genetic information from more than 10,000 Australians with depression.
  • According to recent reports, circadian depression is associated with the body's 24-hour internal clock, which helps regulate when we feel awake and when we feel sleepy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly identified form of depression may help explain why some people struggle to find relief from commonly prescribed antidepressants. Researchers at the University of Sydney have discovered a subtype called "circadian depression," which appears to be closely connected to the body's internal biological clock.

Sources indicate that the discovery emerged from an analysis of clinical and genetic information from more than 10,000 Australians with depression. Nearly one-quarter of the participants in the study, which focused on people with severe, recurrent or persistent depression, showed characteristics of this newly identified subtype.

According to recent reports, circadian depression is associated with the body's 24-hour internal clock, which helps regulate when we feel awake and when we feel sleepy. People with this form of depression tend to respond less favorably to common serotonin-based antidepressants. However, treatments that target the brain circuits involved in controlling circadian rhythms, including melatonin, melatonin-targeted antidepressants and light therapy, may offer more effective options.

Published in the British Journal of Psychiatry, the findings shed light on the genetic factors associated with this subtype and offer a possible explanation for why widely used medications such as SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) are less effective for some patients.

A Hidden Type of Depression Affecting Nearly One in Four Patients Studied.

Industry observers note that to investigate the biological differences between forms of depression, researchers examined information collected through the nationwide Australian Genetics of Depression Study. Their analysis included clinical histories and genetic data from more than 10,000 people who had experienced depression.

The researchers identified nearly 25 percent (2,604 participants) as having circadian depression. Several recognizable patterns distinguished these individuals from other people with depression.

Those with the circadian subtype were more likely to experience seasonal changes in their depression, sleep for longer periods when depressed, and wake up feeling exhausted despite spending more time in bed. They were also more likely to be night owls, meaning they naturally preferred staying awake late and waking later in the day.

In a recent development, the differences extended beyond sleep patterns. Depression often began earlier in life for these individuals, and their symptoms tended to be more severe (such as mania and higher levels of suicidal thoughts). Genetic analysis also revealed an increased predisposition to inflammatory and cardiovascular health problems, along with major neurodevelopmental disorders, including ADHD.

First author Dr. Emiliana Tonini from the University of Sydney's Brain and Mind Center said:.

"Our research has identified circadian depression as a upcoming subtype, affecting around a quarter of people in our study into those with severe, recurrent or persistent depression.

"Depression is not a uniform illness, and understanding the characteristics of different subtypes means that we can give people earlier access to treatments that will be most effective for them.".

Why Common Antidepressants May Be Less Effective.

One of the most important implications of the discovery involves how depression is treated.

According to recent reports, medications such as SSRIs and SNRIs (serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) are generally among the first treatments offered to people diagnosed with depression. These drugs work by influencing chemical messengers in the brain that help regulate mood.

In a recent development, however, the researchers found that these medications tend to be less effective for people with circadian depression. Individuals with this subtype also experience more side effects, suggesting that conventional antidepressants may not be the best initial approach for everyone.

Recent findings suggest that because circadian depression is closely associated with the body's internal clock, therapies designed to influence that clock may be particularly useful. Light therapy, for example, uses controlled exposure to bright light to help regulate biological rhythms. Melatonin, a hormone involved in signaling when the body should prepare for sleep, and antidepressants that target melatonin pathways may also be relevant treatment options.

In a recent development, co-senior author Dr. Jacob Crouse from the Brain and Mind Center explained:.

"Because circadian depression is linked to people's internal body clock, treatments targeting the circadian rhythm, such as light therapy and melatonin, may be much more relevant, and clinicians should reach for these much earlier in people with this presentation.

"For those who find that antidepressants are not working for them, it is important to speak to your clinician for advice about your individual circumstances.".

A Upcoming Approach Could Improve Depression Treatment in Young People.

Recognizing circadian depression earlier could be especially vital for younger patients, who may otherwise spend valuable time trying medications that are less suited to their particular form of depression.

Professor Ian Hickie, Co-Director of the Brain and Mind Centre and a clinical psychiatrist, warned that failing to identify this subtype in young people can contribute to unsuccessful early treatments and unnecessary side effects.

Sources indicate that the findings highlight the importance of recognizing that depression is not a single, uniform condition. Different biological mechanisms may contribute to similar symptoms, meaning that treatments effective for one person may provide much less benefit to another.

By identifying patients whose depression is closely tied to circadian rhythms, clinicians may be able to offer more targeted treatments earlier rather than relying on the same initial medication approach for everyone.

"We really want young people to receive the most appropriate treatment early in their course of illness.

"Most young people will be offered SSRIs first up, but for at least a quarter there are better circadian-focused medical and behavioral options to help treat and manage their condition.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Heartopia has officially shared initial details about its first-ever collaboration event. The game, which introduced a month ago to great success on mobile, as well as Steam on PC, has already been a staple among fans of Animal Crossing and The Sims.

Things are kicking into gear, it seems, because the game is already about to host its first collaboration event, and it is with My Little Pony.

It has been revealed that the Heartopia X My Little Pony event officially begins on February 14, but a pre-launch login event is now live through the actual collaboration’s start. The limited-time event offers players sign-in puzzles every day that will unlock time-limited Exhibition Passes.

The first actual piece of My Little Pony-themed content can be yours if you complete all puzzles, as that gets you a limited edition costume for your pet, based on the show’s Spike. The event itself, which will be available until March 15, brings My Little Pony’s Tree of Harmony into the world of Heartopia.

The ponies need your help to Wield Elements of Harmony so they can reawaken the tree, and bring it back to Equestria. In gameplay terms, you’re going to want to perform daily sensing at the tree in order to earn three of the six Elements of Harmony: Honesty, Generosity, Loyalty, Kindness, Laughter, and Magic.

Industry observers note that the more you do this, the more the tree’s Energy goes up, and the more rewards and resources you stand to earn. Even more time-limited Exhibition Passes, and Moonlight Crystals can be earned as you water the tree.

In a recent development, badge Pull Tokens are your significant reward, which is what you’re actually going to use to get the special Pony Series badges. You’ll earn ten time-limited Exhibition Passes each time you complete one of the three sets of Pony Series badges. Collect all three and you’ll earn Town Collaboration Series badges.

Heartopia is a free-to-play game, so you know there is a Gacha component to this event. Expect six non-replacement Gacha Pools that each map to one member of My Little Pony’s Mane Six. Within each pool, you’ll be able to earn five outfit pieces, and one vehicle.

In a recent development, we also recently updated our guides on how to catch Frostspore fish - and if you’re into cooking, how to obtain every recipe and variant. If you haven’t already, definitely see if you missed any of these Heartopia codes, too.

  • Elon Musk indicates Tesla’s cars don’t need the next-generation AI5 chip, so it’s going to Optimus first.
  • According to Commercial Times, Tesla’s chip design partner Global Unichip (GUC) is giving its limited TSMC 3nm capacity for 2027 to Google and Microsoft data center chips first.
  • Last Sunday, a Tesla owner asked Musk when AI5 would be in newly introduced cars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk indicates Tesla’s cars don’t need the next-generation AI5 chip, so it’s going to Optimus first. A upcoming report from Taiwan’s chip supply chain gives a more practical reason: Tesla won’t have enough AI5 chips for its cars until 2028.

According to Commercial Times, Tesla’s chip design partner Global Unichip (GUC) is giving its limited TSMC 3nm capacity for 2027 to Google and Microsoft data center chips first. That leaves Tesla with a relatively small AI5 allocation.

Last Sunday, a Tesla owner asked Musk when AI5 would be in newly introduced cars. His answer: “It’s going to Optimus. Cars will remain at AI4. That’s enough to solve superhuman driving.”.

As we reported this week, FSD v15 is basically AI4’s last shot. Tesla engineers are already squeezing the last few percent of utilization out of the chip, and the AI4.5 refresh is mostly a move to LPDDR5X memory. Musk stated Tesla cut AI4.5 from 32GB to 24GB of RAM because “RAM is super expensive,” and that AI4 itself now costs twice as much due to memory and storage price hikes.

Recent findings suggest that it’s quite a change in aims. In June 2024, Musk said AI5 would be in vehicles in the second half of 2025. Tesla only taped out AI5 in April, and Musk had already started describing its focus as Optimus and Tesla’s supercomputer clusters.

The Commercial Times report, published today, describes GUC as the custom ASIC design partner on Tesla’s AI5 project. GUC is the design services house whose largest shareholder is TSMC, and it works mostly on data center silicon.

In a recent development, industry sources told the paper that GUC’s 2027 allocation of TSMC’s N3 capacity is much larger than this year’s. But with AI compute demand exploding, it still can’t serve every major customer at once.

It has been revealed that so GUC is prioritizing North American cloud projects, including Google’s Axion 2 and Axion 3 server processors and Microsoft’s in-house chips. Those orders carry high margins and good visibility. Tesla’s robot and car chip doesn’t make the front of the line.

Industry observers note that the result, according to the report, is that Tesla’s initial 2027 wafer quota can’t support annual shipments for a fleet of millions of cars. The supply chain expects that limited AI5 volume to go first to Optimus, which needs a lot of compute but ships in small numbers, and only expects large-scale adoption in cars after N3 capacity expands further in 2028.

TSMC is adding 3nm capacity, but not fast. Its latest 3nm fab in Tainan is scheduled for volume production in the first half of 2027, and its second Arizona fab, which Musk has said will produce AI5, in the second half of 2027.

Tesla does have a second source. Samsung is building its own version of AI5 on 2nm at its Taylor, Texas fab, but it expects volume production of Tesla’s AI chips there in the second half of 2027.

Now look at the numbers. Tesla delivered roughly 1.6 million vehicles last year. Every one of them needs a self-driving computer.

According to recent reports, optimus is a different story. Tesla now plans to put AI5 in Optimus around April 2027 and push external Optimus deliveries to late 2027. Even an aggressive robot ramp next year is measured in thousands of units, not millions.

If your 2027 AI5 supply is a fraction of what a car program needs, Optimus is the only product Tesla has that can absorb it.

Musk’s version is that cars don’t need AI5 because AI4 is “enough to solve superhuman driving.” The supply chain’s version is that Tesla can’t get enough AI5 chips to put in cars anyway. Both can be true at the same time, but only one of them explains the timing.

We failed to secure supply, thus we are turning around 180° and tell you that you don't need our product.*.

*Who cares about former customers. Oh hello HW3 owners.

Sources indicate that look at how Tesla has been handling silicon this fall. It cut AI4.5 RAM. It cut AI5 RAM from 144GB to 72GB, then bumped it to 96GB a day later. It says AI4 costs double what it used to. That’s a manufacturer rationing chips and memory, not one choosing to leave a 12x compute upgrade on the shelf because it isn’t needed.

And if AI4 really were plenty, Tesla engineers wouldn’t be talking about squeezing out the last few percent of the chip for v15.

Industry observers note that so here’s how we read it. Tesla had to pick where its scarce AI5 chips go in 2027, and it picked the low-volume product. “AI4 is enough” is the story that makes that decision sound like a choice. And it’s a story we heard about HW3, Tesla’s previous self-driving computer.

Industry News: Upcoming gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1117 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers in Japan have developed a promising newly introduced treatment for gum disease that kills harmful bacteria while leaving beneficial microbes unharmed.
  • Developed by scientists at Nagoya University, the treatment combines antibodies obtained from egg yolks with near-infrared light.
  • Why Conventional Gum Disease Treatments Can Cause Problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers in Japan have developed a promising newly introduced treatment for gum disease that kills harmful bacteria while leaving beneficial microbes unharmed. Unlike conventional approaches that can eliminate both good and bad bacteria, the new therapy is designed to target specific microbes responsible for damaging gums and the bone that supports teeth.

Developed by scientists at Nagoya University, the treatment combines antibodies obtained from egg yolks with near-infrared light. Early experiments in human cell cultures and mice suggest that it could offer a more precise way to combat periodontitis, a serious form of gum disease that can eventually lead to tooth loss. The findings were published in the Journal of Translational Medicine.

Why Conventional Gum Disease Treatments Can Cause Problems.

Industry observers note that the human mouth contains a complex community of microorganisms, many of which play important roles in maintaining oral health. Problems can arise when harmful bacteria multiply and disturb this delicate balance.

One particularly troublesome species is Porphyromonas gingivalis (P. gingivalis), which scientists classify as a keystone pathogen. This means it can have an outsized influence on the surrounding microbial community, even when it is not especially abundant. By promoting inflammation and disrupting the normal balance of oral bacteria, it can contribute to the destruction of the bone that holds teeth in place.

Sources indicate that treating periodontitis often involves eliminating the bacteria responsible for the infection. However, some existing antimicrobial treatments do not distinguish between harmful organisms and microbes that help maintain a healthy mouth.

"Current treatments for periodontitis, including antibiotics and antimicrobial photodynamic therapy (aPDT), eliminate both pathogenic and beneficial oral bacteria," remarked Kazuhide Sato, one of the corresponding authors and a lecturer at Nagoya University. "These approaches often disrupt the entire oral microbial ecosystem and can also release lipopolysaccharide (LPS), an endotoxin that may exacerbate inflammation.".

Scientists Adapt Cancer Therapy to Target Gum Disease Bacteria.

To overcome these limitations, the Nagoya University team turned to a technology originally designed to treat cancer. Known as near-infrared photoimmunotherapy, it uses antibodies linked to a light-sensitive dye to recognize specific targets. Once the compound attaches to its intended target, exposure to near-infrared light activates the dye and produces a damaging effect.

It has been revealed that the researchers adapted this strategy to attack P. gingivalis without unnecessarily disturbing other oral bacteria. Their approach relies on IgY, a type of antibody collected from the egg yolks of hens that have been immunized against the pathogen.

Egg yolk antibodies offer a practical advantage because they can be produced in large quantities at relatively low cost. This could make them an attractive option for developing targeted treatments that are affordable and scalable.

The resulting technology, called near-infrared photo-antibacterial targeting therapy (NIR-PAT²), was developed by researchers at Nagoya University Graduate School of Medicine. The team included first author Hiroshi Maruyama, Professor Hideharu Hibi, and corresponding authors Sato and Kiyoshi Sakai.

To determine whether the treatment could destroy harmful bacteria while protecting healthy tissue, the researchers tested it in human cell cultures and mice. They also compared its effects with those of conventional antimicrobial therapies.

Light-Activated Antibodies Destroy Harmful Bacteria.

Laboratory experiments highlighted that the antibody and dye combination attached specifically to P. gingivalis. Other bacterial species and healthy human gum cells were left unaffected.

When the researchers illuminated the targeted bacteria with near-infrared light, the activated dye damaged their outer membranes, ultimately killing them.

Sources indicate that microscopic examination revealed an key difference between this technique and conventional antimicrobial light therapy. Bacteria exposed to the fresh treatment developed tiny openings in their membranes but largely maintained their overall shape. By contrast, conventional antimicrobial photodynamic therapy caused the bacteria to break apart completely.

Industry observers note that the distinction matters because destroying bacterial cells can release substances that contribute to inflammation. Preserving the overall structure of the targeted bacteria, even after killing them, could help limit this unwanted effect.

The researchers also examined how the treatments affected healthy human gum cells. Their targeted therapy caused no detectable harm to these cells, while conventional antimicrobial photodynamic therapy produced cellular damage and slowed healing.

New Treatment Reduces Bone Loss in Mice.

The team next investigated whether these laboratory findings would translate into meaningful improvements in gum disease.

In mice with periodontitis, the experimental therapy significantly reduced the loss of alveolar bone, the part of the jawbone that surrounds and supports teeth. Preventing this type of bone deterioration is especially crucial because advanced periodontitis can loosen teeth and eventually cause them to fall out.

Analysis of the animals' saliva revealed another encouraging result. The treatment reduced P. gingivalis while preserving beneficial Streptococcus bacteria, helping maintain a healthier balance of microorganisms in the mouth.

Conventional antibiotics and antimicrobial photodynamic therapy, on the other hand, eliminated both harmful and beneficial bacteria in the experiments, causing broader disruption to the oral microbial community.

"Results demonstrated that, unlike antibiotics or standard light therapy, this approach selectively removes the primary pathogenic species while preserving the remainder of the oral bacterial community," Sato said.

Together, the findings suggest that targeting individual disease-causing bacteria could help control gum disease while avoiding some of the unintended consequences of broader antimicrobial treatments.

AI Could Help Develop More Precise Gum Disease Treatments.

In a recent development, although the early results are promising, the researchers recognize that periodontitis is a complex disease involving multiple bacterial species. Eliminating P. gingivalis alone may not be sufficient to treat every case.

To address this challenge, the team prepares to use artificial intelligence (AI) to examine publicly available information about oral bacteria. By identifying other key microorganisms and studying how different species interact, they hope to uncover additional targets for future therapies.

The researchers also see potential implications beyond oral health. Periodontitis has been linked to several other medical conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis and diabetes.

Understanding the relationships between oral bacteria and these conditions could eventually help scientists identify which patients are most likely to benefit from specific treatments. AI analysis may play a role in making those decisions and guiding the development of more personalized approaches to gum disease.

For now, the therapy remains experimental, with its effectiveness demonstrated in laboratory studies and mice rather than human clinical trials. However, the findings point toward a possible future in which treating gum disease means selectively removing harmful bacteria instead of disrupting the entire microbial community that helps keep the mouth healthy.

It is also, quite visibly, the most popular Nioh release ever on PC, and it was impressive watching more and more players jump into the game over the weekend and push the numbers higher.

Nioh 3 came out swinging, breaking the series’ Steam concurrent player record immediately after lanch, with 42,822. Anyone keeping up with how well the game has been received, and how much it’s been anticipated by series fans and Soulslike players, would’ve told you that it was only the beginning.

Recent findings suggest that that’s an incredibly healthy player base, but more than that, it’s more than double the previous record holder, Nioh 2, which peaked at 41,325 concurrent players in 2021.
