💡 Key Takeaways
  • Latest multiplayer game Spirit Crossing offers up a visually blissful, but inwardly draconian world in which other people are not allowed to talk to you – indeed, not permitted access to the visible electromagnetic spectrum – unless you have given them a high five.
  • In a recent development, deign to slap somebody's hand, and they'll pop into colour and be able to join you for various activities.
  • Recent findings suggest that there's nothing forcing you to do any of this in manufacturer, mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest multiplayer game Spirit Crossing offers up a visually blissful, but inwardly draconian world in which other people are not allowed to talk to you – indeed, not permitted access to the visible electromagnetic spectrum – unless you have given them a high five. By default, players appear to each other as shadows, all exploring a skybound landscape of magic animals and layer-cake mountains that reminds me of both Sable and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

In a recent development, deign to slap somebody's hand, and they'll pop into colour and be able to join you for various activities. For example, going fishing, playing instruments round the campfire, playing dress-up and pulling emotes in group photos, bouncing around on strangely inflated yaks, or questing forth to heal troubled spirits. There's some material gathering and crafting, and there are recurring storms that make the ambience more threatening, but overcoming a challenge doesn't feel like the point of Spirit Crossing. The "missions" are just an excuse to hang out together.

Recent findings suggest that there's nothing forcing you to do any of this in manufacturer, mind. "Stay a mysterious shadow, lend a hand when you feel like it, and disappear before anyone can make it weird," the devs explain, adding a hug emoji to make plain that they don't think you're some kind of smelly misanthrope for shunning other players.

I, personally, am a smelly misanthrope, and will only ever appear in your game as a skulking opacity, peering through the window of your personal gingerbread house, with its tastefully accessorised lava lamps and throw rugs. No, I will not join you for a group hang-glider tour. No, I do not want to play the banjo with you. You will experience me only as the nagging sensation of being watched, while you chat to the local "Stylesmith" about fetching rucksack patterns.

In a recent development, spirit Crossing has an upfront cost that "gives players full access to the complete game experience in perpetuity", but you can also take out a subscription for some cosmetic items and access to a "limited resource exchange shop". They're avoiding traditional microtransactions, which is nice.

Sources indicate that spry Fox are also the developers of Cozy Grove - "the best grove since Byker", wrote Graham, in one of his regular 'senior moments'. I myself know them as the studio behind wintry puzzler Road Not Taken, with its randomised woodlands, and block-merging city builder Triple Town, with its unexpectedly terrifying bears. Little about Spirit Crossing seems terrifying, unless you count the shadow loitering at the edge of your conversation pit.

Sources indicate that you can read more about the game on Steam. I find Spirit Crossing quite novel, especially when it dispenses with the WholeCosy "discover your inner fashonista" stuff and leans into the supernatural elements: I like the idea of hunkering by the campfire during a storm, watching the clouds hurtle past. Still, I'm disappointed to hear that Spry Fox have made use of generative AI during its creation.

According to recent reports, as has been pointed out to us on Bluesky, the developers called on Anthropic's Claude tools for various behind-the-scenes tasks - the example they give in a Discord post is editing several config files at once. There's no disclosure on the game's Steam page because Spry Fox haven't used AI tools to generate any of the art or music - Valve rewrote Steam's disclosure requirements in January to exempt the usage of generative AI for "efficiency gains", which the above presumably falls under.

Recent findings suggest that it's hardly a full-throated endorsement of generative AI, but it still forms part of a political and cultural project I consider reckless and morbid. For a longer account of my objections, albeit one that doesn't cover Claude in particular, here's my longform thinkywangle from July last year.

#224104. Latest Update: What did the Soviet Union's final deep space probe actually see on Mars?

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Space ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: What did the Soviet Union's final deep space probe actually see on Mars?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1568 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, on July 12, 1988, Phobos 2 — one of the Soviet Union's final major planetary exploration probes — was debuted from Baikonur Cosmodrome aboard a Proton rocket.
  • However, early in the following year, the spacecraft's mission abruptly ended after the Phobos 2 ground team mysteriously lost contact with the spacecraft.
  • So what caused the odd-looking appearance of the shadow in the final images captured by Phobos 2, and what was the real reason behind the spacecraft's sudden failure?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on July 12, 1988, Phobos 2 — one of the Soviet Union's final major planetary exploration probes — was debuted from Baikonur Cosmodrome aboard a Proton rocket. The spacecraft's mission included the study of Mars and the Martian moon Phobos, with a planned close approach and deployment of landing probes, and over the next several months, the spacecraft successfully captured more than three dozen images of Phobos during its time in service.

However, early in the following year, the spacecraft's mission abruptly ended after the Phobos 2 ground team mysteriously lost contact with the spacecraft. Adding to the mystery were objects in some of the final photographs dispatched by the doomed spacecraft, which seemed to show an elongated shadow beneath the probe — a strange twist in one of the Soviet Union's final space missions, and one that soon gave rise to conspiracy theories about what the fate of Phobos 2 might have been.

So what caused the odd-looking appearance of the shadow in the final images captured by Phobos 2, and what was the real reason behind the spacecraft's sudden failure?

Originally, the Soviet Union had planned for Phobos 2 to reach the Red Planet by late January 1989, after which the spacecraft would begin collecting data about the Martian environment leading up to its initial contact with Mars' largest moon in early June.

To say that a lot hinged on the success of the mission would be an understatement, given the unfortunate fate of the probe's predecessor, Phobos 1, which went offline on Sept. 2, 1988, after a faulty command sequence was initiated while the spacecraft was on its way to Mars. The stakes were almost immediately raised as Phobos 2 arrived in orbit around Mars on Jan. 30, 1989, when one of the probe's three onboard flight system processors was found to have gone offline, with another already experiencing technical challenges.

Sources indicate that over the course of the next several weeks, Phobos 2 was able to overcome some of these setbacks and successfully began sending useful scientific data about the Martian environment back to Earth. By March, all the probe's science instruments appeared to be functioning normally, and despite the earlier loss of one of its processors, the remaining two had continued to facilitate control of the spacecraft by its Soviet ground control team.

That all changed on March 27, 1989, as Phobos 2 prepared to capture navigational images of its namesake as the Martian moon passed, which would be useful in advance of another forthcoming flyby in early April.

It has been revealed that achieving this meant that the probe had to be angled in such a way that it faced Phobos, whereby its communications antennas would be temporarily directed away from Earth. During the imaging portion of the maneuver, all appeared to go smoothly, but soon afterward, ground controllers realized they were unable to reestablish contact with the probe.

It has been revealed that A few fleeting radio contacts were made over the ensuing hours, which engineers believed might indicate that during the period of signal loss required for imagery of Phobos to be obtained, the spacecraft may have begun to spin uncontrollably. If this were the case, and the spacecraft could not reorient its solar panels toward the sun, it would eventually lose all power.

Recent findings suggest that no further contact with Phobos 2 could be established beyond this point, although images from the probe's final close encounter with the Martian moon were successfully delivered back to Soviet ground controllers. While investigators identified a failure involving the spacecraft's onboard computer system as the most probable explanation, to this day, the exact cause of the events leading to the loss remains unknown.

In a recent development, although questions remain about the fate of Phobos 2, several theories have been put forward over the years. According to authors Paolo Ulivi and David M. Harland, one of the simplest explanations was that the spacecraft was damaged after an impact with other material orbiting the Martian moon, although later modeling by Soviet engineers and American teams at NASA's Jet Propulsion Lab seemed to rule this out.

A more likely scenario involved failure of the probe's second attitude control computer, which had already begun experiencing technical concerns as Phobos 2 arrived in Martian orbit. With two of its three processors now offline, the third and sole remaining computer was unable to maintain control of the spacecraft on its own. An additional factor might have been power loss from battery drainage while the probe's solar arrays were directed away from the sun, and with no failsafe to power down any non-critical systems under such conditions, the spacecraft would likely have undergone significant power loss.

However, the probe's failure was only one part of the mystery: equally perplexing had been the unusual images Phobos 2 captured in its final moments, which later sparked speculation — and conspiracy theories — about what might have been behind the spacecraft's sudden demise.

In some of the final images captured by Phobos 2, an unusual, elongated shadow had been visible in the frame, which with time would begin to prompt the most unusual of all the theories about the probe's demise: that it had been disabled by an alien spacecraft.

According to recent reports, among the proponents of this theory had been Marina Popovich, a former experimental pilot and the first Soviet woman to break the sound barrier, who set over 100 world aviation records in her career. In 1991, Popovich held a press conference at the Soviet Consulate in San Francisco, where she claimed a cigar-shaped object had been photographed near the Martian moon, which she believed to be an alien mothership.

In a recent development, given her storied background in Soviet aerospace history, Popovich's views likely carried a degree of credibility unlike most others. However, that did not make them accurate.

Determining what the images actually show requires an understanding of the probe's orbit, particularly with relation to the Martian moon it was attempting to photograph. At the time, the spacecraft and Phobos were in almost the same orbit, and moving at very similar speeds. As Ulivi and Harland note, due to these conditions, the probe's Termoskan multispectral imager often captured images that "included the shadow of the moon on the planet's surface as a dark oblong cigar-shaped feature.".

In 1991, a NASA-led study of the Termoskan observations concluded that the unusual appearance of the shadow most likely resulted from a combination of factors acting together. The study team attributed these to the scanning instrument itself, as well as the spacecraft's near-co-orbital motion with Phobos, its viewing direction, and finally, a slight rocking motion the researchers concluded the spacecraft had likely exhibited at the time.

Sources indicate that however, another factor that contributed to the appearance of the shadow involves the oblique angle at which the moon's shadow strikes the Martian surface. Because of this, similar imagery depicting an elliptical or elongated shadow cast by Phobos has been obtained since the Phobos 2 mission, with examples including images captured by the High-Resolution Stereo Camera (HRSC) on the ESA's Mars Express spacecraft in 2005.

The loss of Phobos 2 became a controversy for reasons other than the imaginative speculations about what its final images might have captured.

Industry observers note that john M. Logsdon, director of the Space Policy Institute at George Washington University's School of International Affairs, remarked to the Los Angeles Times shortly after the failure that the situation was "just horrible," noting that the mishap was expected to potentially fuel what he called "a first-rate bureaucratic struggle" the Soviet Union was undergoing amid political changes occurring there at the time.

"The scientific community is also facing challenges resulting from the restructuring of the Soviet system," the Times also reported, noting the scientists from more than a dozen nations around the world whose funding and scientific instruments, at an estimated cost of several millions of dollars, "must be counted among the losers in the failure of the probe to complete its basic mission.".

Industry observers note that although both Phobos spacecraft were lost prior to completion of their primary missions, there were still some meaningful scientific results they produced. These included latest data collected about both Mars and Phobo­s which, according to Ulivi and Harland, exceeded the total data collected from all past Soviet missions to the Red Planet.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, the circumstances surrounding the demise of Phobos 2 remain one of the more intriguing episodes in the history of Soviet space exploration. The unusual observations made during its final moments, coupled with lingering questions about precisely what went wrong, have helped sustain decades of speculation.

In a recent development, today, the truncated Phobos 2 mission remains a curious ending note for the Soviet-era space program. It is one that still fuels speculation, and reminds us how swiftly the unknown can take our minds to imaginative places — especially when it comes to mysteries involving space, the cosmos, and the potential existence of life beyond Earth.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A dietary supplement known as urolithin A may help the brain meet its increased demand for oxygen and nutrients during mentally challenging activities.
  • According to recent reports, obesity can affect how blood vessels function, potentially disrupting circulation throughout the body and brain.
  • During a demanding memory exercise, participants who received urolithin A showed a greater increase in brain blood flow than those in the placebo group.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A dietary supplement known as urolithin A may help the brain meet its increased demand for oxygen and nutrients during mentally challenging activities. In a clinical trial led by researchers at the University of Oklahoma, middle-aged adults with obesity who took the supplement experienced increased blood flow to the brain while performing a memory task. The findings, published in JAMA Network Open, could shed new light on how urolithin A influences blood vessel function and brain health.

According to recent reports, obesity can affect how blood vessels function, potentially disrupting circulation throughout the body and brain. To investigate whether urolithin A could help counter these effects, the research team recruited 50 adults with obesity between the ages of 40 and 64 for a randomized clinical trial. For four weeks, participants took either 1,000 milligrams of urolithin A each day or a placebo.

Urolithin A Increases Blood Flow to the Brain.

During a demanding memory exercise, participants who received urolithin A showed a greater increase in brain blood flow than those in the placebo group. The difference was especially noticeable in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, an area that plays an key role in working memory, the ability to temporarily hold and process information.

Industry observers note that however, the researchers observed no significant improvement in blood vessel function in the arm or in participants' performance on memory tests. According to the research team, this is the first study in humans to document an effect of urolithin A on the function of blood vessels in the brain.

Industry observers note that "The brain needs an adequate supply of blood to meet the demands of mental activity," stated the study's first author, Ana Clara da Costa Pinaffi Langley, Ph.D., an assistant professor in the Department of Nutritional Sciences at the OU College of Allied Health on the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus. "We found that urolithin A increased blood flow to the brain during a memory task, suggesting the supplement may help the brain meet its increased need for oxygen and nutrients when it is working harder. We plan to conduct more research to understand what this finding means for brain health.".

A Natural Compound Produced by Gut Bacteria.

The human body can produce urolithin A with the help of certain gut bacteria. These microorganisms generate the substance by breaking down naturally occurring compounds in foods such as pomegranates, strawberries, and walnuts.

According to recent reports, not everyone produces the same amount of urolithin A. Previous research suggests that the ability to generate the compound naturally tends to diminish as people grow older and their body mass index increases, Langley explained. Urolithin A can also be obtained directly through dietary supplements.

It has been revealed that participants tolerated the supplement well throughout the trial. However, the researchers cautioned that the study involved a relatively small number of people at a single research site. Larger, longer clinical trials will be necessary to better understand the supplement's effects.

Could Urolithin A Support Healthier Brain Aging?

Although the increase in brain blood flow is encouraging, it remains unclear whether this change could translate into lasting improvements in cognitive health.

"These findings offer an interesting starting point for understanding how urolithin A affects the brain," said study co-author Andriy Yabluchanskiy, M.D., Ph.D., an associate professor in the Department of Neurosurgery at the OU College of Medicine. "Although we saw increased blood flow to the brain during mental activity, participants did not demonstrate measurable improvements in memory or attention. Future studies will need to determine whether taking the supplement for a longer period leads to meaningful improvements in cognitive function or other health benefits.".

For Langley, the broader aim is to extend healthspan, the portion of a person's life spent in good health.

It has been revealed that "The idea is to mitigate cognitive decline," she said. "We want to expand the time that people are living healthier lives.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • PC players have been conditioned for decades to accept the keyboard-and-mouse setup for RTS games.
  • Unveiled on March 1st 2000 at Microsoft's Gamestock event, the Strategic Commander was one of three additions to their SideWinder line, with a scheduled release that October at a pricey $64.95.
  • In a recent development, microsoft, all the while, were taking notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PC players have been conditioned for decades to accept the keyboard-and-mouse setup for RTS games. One hand has to handle movement and commands through a keyboard, while the other points, drags, and selects with a mouse. Peripheral makers have, usually with the addition of more buttons, made many minor variations to this time-honored arrangement, but there's only ever been one real attempt to rethink it entirely for the PC: the Microsoft SideWinder Strategic Commander.

Unveiled on March 1st 2000 at Microsoft's Gamestock event, the Strategic Commander was one of three additions to their SideWinder line, with a scheduled release that October at a pricey $64.95. At E3 later that May, Microsoft demonstrated the Strategic Commander for the first time with SimCity 3000, while promoting its potential for other such games as Diablo II, Warcraft III, and Baldur's Gate II. This was all taking place during the so-called 'Golden Age of Real-Time Strategy Games,' which spanned roughly from the mid-1990s to the mid-2000s. It was when the RTS genre was at the peak of its mainstream popularity, and we fans were devoted to mastering its intricacies in any way we could to have a competitive edge.

In a recent development, microsoft, all the while, were taking notes. "The team conceived the Strategic Commander in the late 1990s," Carl Ledbetter - then Industrial Design Manager for Microsoft's PC Hardware Group, now Head of Design for Xbox Devices - recalls to me. "As RTS games grew in popularity, we saw an interesting opportunity to design a latest physical interface around a new interaction model. The idea was for it to be used left-handed in concert with right-hand PC desktop mouse control. We wanted to enable players to perform faster with more fluidity, comfort, optimised control placement for multiple hand sizes, simplicity of set-up, and ease of programming.".

For Ledbetter and co. to realise this ambition, the Strategic Commander was designed as a unique combination of mouse, joystick, and gamepad. To manage the increasing complexities of the RTS games of the day, it came equipped with six programmable buttons, three shift buttons, and a three-position profile switch. Back then, these atypical features provided an unprecedented 72 possible key combinations across various configurations, all at the tip of our stubby little fingers. Better yet, it allowed us to toggle between three pre-configured profiles at a time, so that we could switch up our configurations on the fly depending on which stage of an RTS match we were in.

On release, contemporary reviewers acknowledged its originality, with critics like ActiveWin's Julien Jay describing it as "probably the most innovative (with the GameVoice) and revolutionary" peripheral designed specifically for strategy players. Others, like Neoseeker's Arnel Lim, suggested that it might’ve gone overboard with its customisation options, saying "you won't use anywhere close to all of them," in reference to the controller's programmable key combinations. Either way, the Strategic Commander failed to supplant conventional peripherals in the hands of most RTS players, and it was discontinued in 2003. As was the rest of the original SideWinder line, owing to declining sales and the industry-wide shift toward standard M+K setups for all PC games and genres.

According to recent reports, however, unlike so many of its Microsoft-made siblings, this was not the end for the Strategic Commander. Niche as it was, it went on to enjoy a surprisingly long post-shelf life, one that was stretched out by a dedicated cult following - and that continues to this day. But why? Why, after all these years, is this forgotten peripheral from a discontinued line maintaining such a enthusiastic fanbase, years after the industry around it had written it off as a failure?

Sources indicate that the answer lies in software and OS compatibility, as much as the hardware's own appeal. Andreas Weis was the developer of one of the first unofficial patches for the Strategic Commander, allowing players to keep on using it even after the original software stopped being compatible with newer versions the Windows. By that point, the device was a decade old, and well into 'official' obsolescence, yet Weis still answered the call of the Strategic Commander's righteously frustrated - if numerically few - fans. "There was a lot of interest back in the early 2010s in software patches to keep the Strategic Commander functional when the original software for the Strategic Commander stopped working," he explains. "Users were asking around on internet forums about how to get it to work on Windows 7 and Vista machines. Since I was studying computer science at the time, I was quite interested in reverse-engineering, and I hacked together a simple tool that would cover my use cases for the device.".

Sources indicate that in the years that followed, other patches were released to keep the Strategic Commander operational, the most notable of which was Philip Merwarth’s Strategic Engine software in 2013. Unfortunately, they weren’t open-source. Worse was that the protocol for programming the Strategic Commander wasn’t documented anywhere online in a way that was accessible for consumers. This is why Weis realized that he could make a unique contribution.

"I polished my old prototype code for the Strategic Commander software patch and released it as a library, so that other people could use it to write their own applications for programming the tool," he says. "As for me, I released one application that made use of the library publicly, the vJoy feeder application, which allows the device to be used with games that support joystick inputs." Curiously, Weis, by this time and like many others, had found other applications for a device with such a specific selling point, and even continues to use the Strategic Commander sparingly in 2026.

"The production quality of Microsoft hardware at the time was just top-notch, and I love the design of the old SideWinder devices, which is why I did not just throw the thing out when the software stopped working," he tells me. "It was worth keeping around to find new uses for it over the years, and I eventually realized that it makes quite a nice addition to a HOTAS (Hands-On Throttle And Stick) setup, where I could put actions that aren’t time-critical and don't fit well on the throttle on the Strategic Commander instead. For example, when I’m playing Elite Dangerous in VR, I’d put actions like deploying the landing gear on the Strategic Commander to free up buttons on the throttle for actions that were more relevant for combat.".

When looking back at the history of Microsoft’s SideWinder line, it’s easy to call the Strategic Commander a failed experiment, given the fact that most of us are still using the same standard mouse-and-keyboard setup to play RTS games. However, the central premise behind its design philosophy was that the interface between a player and a game could be redesigned to cater to specific genre quirks, and decades following its release, it’s still maintained a coalition of loyal users: some RTS players who believed the Strategic Commander really pulled it off, and those found other uses for the device in other flavours of PC game. And with the matter of modern compatibility, a roadblock for so much retro hardware, bypassed by homemade patches, both camps can continue twisting and clicking their Strategic Commanders unimpeded.

According to recent reports, all the same, I wonder if it might have basked in more conventional success, had Microsoft made more forward-thinking decisions. The Strategic Commander has proven over the years that its unprecedented customisation had applications far beyond what Ledbetter’s team had envisioned, and once the popularity of RTS games settled down, other, similar click-heavy subgenres like MOBAs and Real-Time Tactics got significant as well. Would a more officially maintained, potentially refined Strategic Commander model have served those crowds? I think it might. The narrow focus on RTS games may have also hurt the device's since-demonstrated broader appeal; if Microsoft had fully capitalised on this customisation selling point by communicating its benefits to everyone, not just those playing the single most popular PC genre at the time, it could have provided the blueprint for a proper, long-lived alternative to controllers, mice, and keyboards.

Alas, gaming history is littered with revolutionary peripherals that failed to actually revolutionise the industry surrounding them. The Strategic Commander is no different, but for the fact that it’s had this surprisingly long post-shelf life - and, as a result, the opportunity for insight into what could have been done to salvage the its failures. Still, that unexpected longevity can provide come comfort to the Strategic Commander's creators, as well as its lingering consumers.

Sources indicate that "I think the design made sense for its time, especially with the rising popularity of RTS games," Ledbetter reflects. "Looking back, I would have liked more time to test and refine the Strategic Commander. I’m proud of what we brought to market, and I’m glad to know that it remains beloved by many players to this day.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The major Diablo 4 Developer Revision has indeed delivered the goods.
  • You can tell Blizzard wanted to have a bit of fun with Season of Slaughter, as many of its major features make it look like a limited-time event, but there is plenty to be excited about here.
  • In a recent development, season of Slaughter kicks off March 11, and will run until the following season kicks off April 28, with the launch of the Lord of Hatred expansion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The major Diablo 4 Developer Revision has indeed delivered the goods. One of the livestream’s big topics was, of course, the game’s upcoming mini-season, which is set to kick off next week and run until the launch of Lord of Hatred, the game’s anticipated next expansion.

You can tell Blizzard wanted to have a bit of fun with Season of Slaughter, as many of its major features make it look like a limited-time event, but there is plenty to be excited about here.

In a recent development, season of Slaughter kicks off March 11, and will run until the following season kicks off April 28, with the launch of the Lord of Hatred expansion. Many of the season’s biggest additions were available to preview in the 2.6.0 Public Test Realm.

Patch 2.6.0, as you might have guessed, is the one that will kick off the slaughter next week. The headline feature here is ability to become The Butcher, the iconic in-game boss who randomly invades players’ games.

When you play as The Butcher, you’ll be rewarded the more kills you get in quick succession. Your skills hotbar will transform to become something more fitting of The Butcher, making them more brutal. You’ll also earn a seasonal currency as you play.

Starting the seasonal questline is how you can begin to assume The Butcher’s form. A Taste of Power can be initiated from Gea Kul. Transforming into The Butcher can be done in a few ways. As you play, you’ll earn Meaty Offerings, which can later be spent on Shrines of Slaughter in the newly introduced Helltide. Once activated, the shrine will draw more enemies towards you.

If you never venture into PvP zones in Diablo 4, this season may change your mind. The standard PvP combat that could only be found in Fields of Hatred has been replaced with a Ceremony of Slaughter, a new event that rewards you for killing enemies quickly. See it through and The Butcher’s Idol will spawn, allowing you to transform into it.

Recent findings suggest that elsewhere in the world, you’ll also be able to attain the same power at Slaughterhouses, a latest activity type available this season. Inside, you immediately become The Butcher for the entirety of the run.

In a recent development, the Butcher’s arrival also ties into two of the other Season of Slaughter’s more interesting additions. First, the Killstreak system finally arrives in Diablo 4, rewarding you for being as efficient as possible in carving your way through enemies.

Anyone who played Diablo 3 should be familiar with how it works. It kicks off the moment you get a kill, and has a visible timer where you’ll need continue performing the same action to up your streak. The more kills you get, the more often your timer will refresh.

It has been revealed that there are five tiers to climb through: Killstreak, Carnage, Devastation, Bloodbath, and Massacre. You’re awarded for the tier you manage to reach before the timer runs out. You’ll earn XP and seasonal rep each time a Killstreak is achieved.

The other Butcher-themed addition is Bloodied Items, which is a newly introduced item quality available throughout this season. They play into the Killstreak system to grant you even more power. Bloodied Items come with unique affixes that scale off your Killstreak tier. You’ll see many familiar items in that pool, as any item in the game has a chance to drop as Bloodied. Bloodied Items can also be acquired by earning Fresh Meat.

Even if none of that sounds exciting, you’re probably going to redownload the game for The Paladin free trial, which kicks off alongside the fresh season on March 11. The trial is only available until March 18, and it lets you try out the Paladin class.

According to recent reports, the trial is available across PC, PlayStation, and Xbox. You’ll be able to take the fresh class for a spin, but your progress will be capped at level 25. The Paladin can be permanently unlocked by buying the Lord of Hatred expansion, as it’s one of two classes the expansion is introducing.

The good news is that any progress you make in the free trial will carry over to the full game if/when you buy the expansion.

Season of Slaughter also kicks off a Doom: The Dark Ages collaboration event. As we’ve come to expect, there’s a very limited free component to the collaboration, in the form of the Doom Reliquary. This is essentially a mini-battle pass that includes the Shield Saw skin, Slayer’s Flair, the head of the Cyberdemon as a back trophy and various other smaller bits.

Industry observers note that the more impressive items - such as character skins, will instead be available to purchase for real money. The list includes the Doom Slayer armor, Mecha Dragon Serrat skin for your cat mount, and a Cacodemon pet.

Though the armor skin is cross-class compatible, judging by how much previous collaboration items have cost in Diablo 4, most of us probably won’t be spending that kind of money to get it.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that the class action suit was filed at the United States District Court for the Northern District of California in June this year.
  • Recent findings suggest that the trio of companies deny having colluded, arguing in a new motion to have the case dismissed (thanks, IGN) that this suit simply retreads old ground covered in a previous antitrust case and quoting deceased judge Richard Posner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A judge has denied a motion to dismiss a US lawsuit against chip makers Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron. The suit acccuses the companies of fixing RAM prices and supply, thereby contributing to worsening the effects of the ongoing memory crisis.

Industry observers note that the class action suit was filed at the United States District Court for the Northern District of California in June this year. It accuses Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron of moving in lockstep away from production of consumer-focused DDR3 and DDR4 RAM and towards HBM memory more typically used in AI datacenters. The suit claims that "in a competitive commodity market", "at least one of three large producers, seeing record prices, would expand output of the product whose price was rising", thereby forcing their competitors to either follow suit or risk losing out on customers.

Recent findings suggest that the trio of companies deny having colluded, arguing in a new motion to have the case dismissed (thanks, IGN) that this suit simply retreads old ground covered in a previous antitrust case and quoting deceased judge Richard Posner. "[C]ompetitors in concentrated markets watch each other like hawks," was the Posner quote they wheeled out, which I mention because otherwise the response I'm about to lay out will sound like a very weird tangent.

Sources indicate that "But Plaintiffs’ allegations go beyond hawks watching each other," judge Noël Wise wrote in her order to deny the dismissal motion. "Their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation – an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do.".

Sources indicate that you know a case is getting serious when facts about Avian behaviour start being wheeled out in response to similes. Bird chatter aside, all this decision means is that the case will rumble on, with both sides still having a chance to present more evidence or make points in their favour before any eventual decision is made by the courts.

So, shelve any hopes you might have of a rapid solution to the memory crisis, which currently looks likely to last until at least 2028.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A upcoming set of Nintendo patents has been discovered that have paved the way for DS, 3DS, and Wii U games to return on Switch 2, so long as the player doesn’t mind shelling out for extra hardware.
  • It has been revealed that the Nintendo DS was a massively popular system, selling 154 million units worldwide.
  • It has been revealed that one possible solution to Nintendo’s second screen matter may have been revealed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A upcoming set of Nintendo patents has been discovered that have paved the way for DS, 3DS, and Wii U games to return on Switch 2, so long as the player doesn’t mind shelling out for extra hardware.

It has been revealed that the Nintendo DS was a massively popular system, selling 154 million units worldwide. However, the system’s dual-screen design has made it hard for its titles to be rereleased on modern systems. Konami managed it with the Castlevania series, but few other companies seem interested in reviving their DS games on the Switch or Switch 2.

It has been revealed that one possible solution to Nintendo’s second screen matter may have been revealed. According to RetroDodo, two patents have been discovered that will allow the Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 to play games from the previous console generations.

The first patent allows a game to be instantly transferred between two systems, while the second allows a different console to be used alongside one running a title, with the ability to use touchscreen controls. Taken together, these patents could emulate the Nintendo DS, 3DS, and Wii U GamePad.

According to recent reports, the caveat is that it would require someone to own two Nintendo Switch 2 units, or one of each Switch console, to run old games. This would be fine in a household that owns both systems, but for those who don’t, it’s an expensive proposition just to be able to run DS, 3DS, and Wii U titles.

This isn’t the first time Nintendo has brought dual-screen games to consoles; DS games were available on the Wii U, with the GamePad used as the bottom screen. This isn’t the most elegant of solutions, especially as it forces the player to keep switching perspective between screens, but it gets the job done.

The caveat to these patents is that it would require someone owning two Nintendo Switch 2 units, or one of each Switch console, to run old games.

Recent findings suggest that there’s also the question of what games fans would even want to play on such a setup. The obvious answer is the Pokémon games, as fans would crawl through broken glass for modern ports of Pokémon HeartGold & SoulSilver that don’t cost hundreds of dollars on eBay. However, considering Game Freak seems averse to making money, there are still easier-to-port Pokémon games that aren’t on the Switch 2, and the DS games would take a ton of work to update.

Industry observers note that the Wii U also doesn’t have much, since pretty much all its best games are already on the Switch, and they received updated ports over the console’s lifespan. Sure, it’d be cool for Nintendo Land to return, but no one’s lining up for Star Fox Zero. The Wii U was such a bomb that Nintendo is unlikely to bring up its ghost, even through a costly hardware expansion.

It has been revealed that the Nintendo 3DS had a stacked library of amazing games, but some of them would lose the system's big selling point: 3D visuals. Super Mario 3D Land was a tremendous game, but it requires playing in 3D to get the full effect, especially for its stage secrets. The lack of Streepass and Spotpass would also take away a lot of the extra functions present in Nintendo 3DS games.

Sources indicate that it’s entirely possible that these Nintendo Switch 2 patents won’t come to anything. After all, companies patent ideas all the time that never get made. The ability to play DS, 3DS, and Wii U games on the Switch 2 would be incredible, but the price of entry might be a bit too high for most fans, even if the titles are released for free on Nintendo Switch Online.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanks to a meaty, well-produced Diablo 4 Developer Patch, we got to have our promised first look at gameplay of the Warlock, the second of two classes coming to the game with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion.

The showcase offered a deep look at the Warlock’s core archetypes, its gameplay and skills loop, and where the class sits within the game’s existing roster of diverse classes.

Recent findings suggest that since the initial reveal of Lord of Hatred, The Warlock has remained the mysterious second class. Anyone who pre-purchased the expansion was able to get immediate access to The Paladin, the other class arriving with the expansion. It wasn’t until February that Blizzard officially revealed the class to the world, but we had to wait until this most recent Developer Revision to actually see it in action.

The Warlock’s pragmatism exists as the counterpart to The Paladin's purity, in that Warlocks don’t shy away from harnessing the powers of Hell to eliminate their enemies. The class can conjure up demons to do their bidding, and utilise attacks previously only available to legions of Hell.

The Warlock is a hybrid pet and caster class. Their gameplay revolves around summoning demons, and undermining enemies with shadow arts. They rely on two resources: Wrath, and Dominance. Casting Skills consumes Wrath, whereas Dominance is what allows the Warlock to summon and exploit demons.

The Warlock has four archetypes players can spec into. Legions are traditional summoners who rely on overwhelming numbers to crush enemies. Vanguards are closer to Sorcerers, capable of dealing damage head-on. Masterminds utilise shadowcraft to slowly drain their enemies. Finally, Ritualists are summoners of the most terrifying Hell demons.

The Warlock is able to do this by fusing Soul Shards into their bodies. Going down any of the four paths becomes available after reaching level 30, which is when the class mechanic is unlocked. Each Soul Shard is tied to a certain demon, and its through that power that the Warlock is able to call upon them in combat. Your choice does, of course, affect your abilities going forward.

Warlocks arrive alongside upcoming Uniques that cater to their specific playstyles, which is similar to what we’ve previously seen with The Paladin, and The Spiritborn before that.

Lord of Hatred arrives April 28. While we wait, Diablo 4’s next season is kicking off next week to deliver a bit of mindless fun to hold us over until the significant day.

#224095. Common supplements rival antibiotics in treating severe gum disease

Common supplements rival antibiotics in treating severe gum disease

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1546 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A familiar dietary supplement combined with low-dose aspirin may offer an unexpected alternative to antibiotics for people with severe gum disease.
  • The findings, published in the Journal of Periodontology, come from researchers affiliated with Albert Einstein Israelite Hospital, Guarulhos University (UNG), the University of Taubaté (UNITAU), and the Ribeirão Preto School of Dentistry at USP (FORP-USP) in Brazil, as well as Harvard University in the United States.
  • Sources indicate that the study suggests that combining omega-3 with low-dose acetylsalicylic acid (ASA), better known as aspirin, could reduce the need for antibiotics in certain patients.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A familiar dietary supplement combined with low-dose aspirin may offer an unexpected alternative to antibiotics for people with severe gum disease. In a year-long clinical trial, patients who received omega-3 and aspirin alongside conventional periodontal treatment experienced nearly identical clinical benefits to those who received antibiotics. Perhaps even more surprisingly, the improvements were still evident six months after supplementation ended.

The findings, published in the Journal of Periodontology, come from researchers affiliated with Albert Einstein Israelite Hospital, Guarulhos University (UNG), the University of Taubaté (UNITAU), and the Ribeirão Preto School of Dentistry at USP (FORP-USP) in Brazil, as well as Harvard University in the United States.

Sources indicate that the study suggests that combining omega-3 with low-dose acetylsalicylic acid (ASA), better known as aspirin, could reduce the need for antibiotics in certain patients. The discovery is particularly timely given growing worldwide concerns about antibiotic resistance, which occurs when bacteria develop the ability to survive exposure to drugs designed to kill them.

Why Severe Gum Disease Is So Difficult To Treat.

Researchers monitored 109 patients with advanced periodontitis over 12 months. Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease that develops when bacteria accumulate below the gumline, triggering an immune response that can gradually damage the tissues and bone that hold teeth in place. Without proper treatment, the disease can cause teeth to loosen and eventually fall out.

As periodontitis progresses, spaces known as periodontal pockets form between the teeth and gums. These pockets can become increasingly deep, making it difficult to remove harmful bacteria through ordinary brushing and flossing.

"Patients with severe disease have very deep pockets, which act as reservoirs for bacteria associated with the disease. It's a very challenging condition to treat," claims dental surgeon Nídia Cristina Castro dos Santos, the first author of the study and a professor and researcher at Einstein.

Putting Omega-3 and Aspirin to the Test.

The researchers randomly divided the participants into four treatment groups. Every patient received subgingival instrumentation, commonly referred to as scaling. This standard periodontal treatment involves removing bacterial deposits and hardened plaque from tooth surfaces beneath the gums. Each group also received a different complementary treatment.

Patients in the control group received inactive substitutes for the antibiotics, omega-3, and aspirin, supplied in capsules that looked identical to those containing the active treatments.

A second group received metronidazole and amoxicillin three times daily for 14 days. This combination of antibiotics has some of the strongest scientific evidence supporting its use as an additional treatment for severe periodontitis.

Sources indicate that participants in the third group took three grams of omega-3 each day, together with a daily dose of low-dose aspirin, for six months. The fourth group received both interventions, taking antibiotics for two weeks while following the six-month omega-3 and aspirin regimen.

The researchers assessed the patients' progress at three, six, and 12 months.

Omega-3 and Aspirin Rival Antibiotics.

At the end of the study, approximately 58% of patients in the antibiotic group had reached the researchers' clinical treatment target, defined as having no more than four remaining deep periodontal pockets.

In a recent development, the omega-3 and aspirin group achieved an almost identical success rate of 57.7%. By comparison, only 23.1% of patients who underwent scaling and received placebos reached the same target. Interestingly, administering both antibiotics and the omega-3 and aspirin regimen together did not produce any additional benefits.

Although antibiotics can improve treatment outcomes in patients with particularly severe gum disease, they are not routinely necessary for everyone with periodontitis.

According to recent reports, "The use of antibiotics isn't considered the gold standard of treatment. Although metronidazole and amoxicillin yield good results in the most severe cases, their use should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis due to risks related to bacterial resistance and possible adverse effects," indicates Castro dos Santos.

Helping the Body Naturally Resolve Inflammation.

According to recent reports, the findings build on earlier research into the potential role of omega-3 fatty acids in protecting oral health. In a previous investigation, also supported by FAPESP and published in Scientific Reports, scientists found that omega-3 supplementation reduced periodontal inflammation and bone loss in rats. The protective effects were particularly notable when supplementation was combined with physical exercise.

Although results from animal studies do not necessarily translate directly to humans, the earlier findings provided clues that omega-3 might help regulate the inflammatory processes that contribute to gum disease.

It has been revealed that omega-3 fatty acids are a group of fats found in foods such as oily fish and are widely available as dietary supplements. Beyond their nutritional importance, they serve as building blocks for certain molecules that help regulate inflammation.

Industry observers note that castro explains that omega-3 works differently from conventional anti-inflammatory medications. Instead of simply interfering with pathways that promote inflammation, omega-3 helps the body produce molecules involved in bringing inflammation to a natural conclusion and supporting tissue repair.

Recent findings suggest that this process, known as the resolution of inflammation, is an active biological mechanism that helps the body return to normal after an immune response. In chronic inflammatory diseases such as periodontitis, inflammation can persist and contribute to ongoing tissue damage.

The researchers included low-dose aspirin because it can promote the formation of certain inflammation-resolving molecules. They suspected that combining aspirin with omega-3 could strengthen the body's ability to control the persistent inflammation associated with advanced gum disease.

Benefits That Lasted Beyond Treatment.

The researchers had originally expected antibiotics and the omega-3 regimen to work best when administered together. Instead, the findings revealed that targeting inflammation could produce clinical improvements comparable to those achieved through antibiotic treatment.

"We imagined that the combination of antibiotics and omega-3 would be most effective in controlling periodontitis in these patients. We also believed that the results for the group that used omega-3 with ASA would be slightly lower than those for the antibiotic group. The result was surprising because the two therapies performed very similarly, paving the way for it to become a treatment option for these patients," claims Castro.

Industry observers note that equally intriguing was how long the improvements lasted. Six months after patients stopped taking omega-3 and aspirin, their clinical outcomes remained similar to those observed when the treatment ended.

In a recent development, according to Castro, this persistence raises the possibility that adjusting the body's inflammatory response could have lasting therapeutic effects. However, scientists are still working to understand the biological mechanisms responsible.

A Potential Alternative Amid Rising Antibiotic Resistance.

For dental surgeon Magda Feres, the study's lead author and a full professor at the Harvard School of Dental Medicine and the Graduate Program in Dentistry at UNG, targeting the body's inflammatory response could provide a valuable treatment option for certain patients.

"The combination of omega-3 and low-dose aspirin achieved clinical benefits comparable to those of the metronidazole and amoxicillin protocol, opening up a real alternative for those who can't take antibiotics, especially patients with allergies or intolerance to these medications," she indicates.

Recent findings suggest that the potential to reduce antibiotic use has implications that extend well beyond dentistry. Antibiotic resistance ranks among the greatest threats to global public health, making it increasingly crucial to identify effective treatment strategies that do not depend on these medications.

"Demonstrating that it's possible to treat severe periodontitis by modulating the body's own response is latest and relevant information that helps preserve antibiotics for when they are truly indispensable," says Feres.

More Research Is Needed Before Clinical Practice Changes.

It has been revealed that despite the encouraging findings, the researchers caution that the results are not sufficient to justify an immediate change in how dentists treat severe periodontitis. The participants did not have other significant systemic or oral diseases, meaning the results may not apply equally to patients with additional health conditions.

Larger studies involving more diverse populations will be needed to validate the findings and determine which patients are most likely to benefit from each treatment strategy.

It has been revealed that it is also important to recognize that omega-3 and aspirin were used alongside professional periodontal treatment, rather than as a substitute for it. Aspirin carries potential risks, including an increased risk of bleeding, and may not be appropriate for everyone.

Meanwhile, Feres and her colleagues are investigating how the different treatments affect the communities of bacteria living inside periodontal pockets. Early microbiological findings point to a decline in bacterial species associated with periodontal disease and an increase in microorganisms linked to healthier gums.

These ongoing investigations could help explain why targeting inflammation produced such promising results and whether the approach can reliably benefit a broader range of patients.

In a recent development, "It's an crucial step forward, but not the end of the story. Therefore, the message is one of cautious optimism: we have a promising, scientifically plausible alternative to antibiotics in select cases. Routine replacement will require more evidence," she concludes.

Star Wars Galactic Racer will get local split-screen multiplayer in early 2027 with new 'Free Play' mode, finally letting racers yell at one another in a tangible space

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Split-screen multiplayer is often treated by developers as a forgotten vestige of a bygone age, something to be left behind as the standardisation of online play makes it redundant, especially following the pandemic.
  • In a recent development, this newly introduced mode, Free Play, not only allows for local multiplayer of up to four players (with either humans or CPUs racing together), but also for complete freedom of choice in vehicle, character and planet to race on.
  • As for why this feature may not have been available at launch, other than the cynical view that it wasn't considered a moneymaking priority for Fuse Games and Secret Mode, CD Projekt Red senior technical producer Shayna Moon weighed in to theorise that it took some effort to get four separately-rendered views of the game running without making their machine explode like the Death Star.

Split-screen multiplayer is often treated by developers as a forgotten vestige of a bygone age, something to be left behind as the standardisation of online play makes it redundant, especially following the pandemic. It's considered unlikely that you'll have another human being in your home to pick up a controller with you, and since you've inevitably got an internet connection, why not just use that to connect to anyone in the world? I find there's a unique beauty in playing something shoulder to shoulder on a couch with another person, and it seems Fuse Games sees that light too, with Star Wars: Galactic Racer set to be updated to add local splitscreen multiplayer sometime early next year.

In a recent development, this newly introduced mode, Free Play, not only allows for local multiplayer of up to four players (with either humans or CPUs racing together), but also for complete freedom of choice in vehicle, character and planet to race on. A simple versus mode like this is a far cry from the roguelite structure of the main game, and one that draws it closer to its arcade racing game roots. An embracing of that is always welcome, as Galactic Racer has been a reminder to many of just how wonderful the arcade racing genre can be, and how poorly served its been in the industry for a while. For example, while the Fuse Games team is partly made up of Criterion Games veterans, Criterion itself has recently been folded into being a Battlefield Studio by EA, making the future of Need for Speed and Burnout uncertain.

As for why this feature may not have been available at launch, other than the cynical view that it wasn't considered a moneymaking priority for Fuse Games and Secret Mode, CD Projekt Red senior technical producer Shayna Moon weighed in to theorise that it took some effort to get four separately-rendered views of the game running without making their machine explode like the Death Star. As Moon puts it: "To be overly simple about it, if the game is running at 30fps for each player, that means it’s actually rendering 120fps." Likely not an issue for a lot of PC players, but a potential issue for console players considering the game is built to run at a locked 60fps for one player on consoles. Past this upcoming upgrade, it looks like the Star Wars franchise as a whole could be set for more smaller games ala Galactic Racer in general, per comments made by Lucasfilms' vice president.

A fat-burning molecule has an unexpected benefit for your muscles

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, researchers have identified a naturally occurring molecule that plays a crucial role in building muscle strength and improving physical performance.
  • Sources indicate that the molecule, known as L-β-aminoisobutyric acid (L-BAIBA), is essential for muscles to adapt to physical activity.
  • The study, published in Nature Communications and funded by Diabetes UK and the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBSRC), reveals that L-BAIBA is a central regulator of the biological changes that allow muscles to improve their strength, structure, and endurance in response to exercise training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, researchers have identified a naturally occurring molecule that plays a crucial role in building muscle strength and improving physical performance. Released during exercise, the molecule could also provide the basis for future treatments to protect against muscle damage associated with type 2 diabetes.

Sources indicate that the molecule, known as L-β-aminoisobutyric acid (L-BAIBA), is essential for muscles to adapt to physical activity. It helps muscles become stronger, improves their resistance to fatigue, and protects against damage and weakness.

The study, published in Nature Communications and funded by Diabetes UK and the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBSRC), reveals that L-BAIBA is a central regulator of the biological changes that allow muscles to improve their strength, structure, and endurance in response to exercise training.

How Exercise Triggers a Natural Muscle Booster.

Although the health benefits of exercise are well established, scientists still do not fully understand the biological processes that allow the body to adapt to physical demands. A research team led by Professor Lee Roberts at the University of Leeds investigated whether these processes could reveal new ways to treat chronic conditions such as type 2 diabetes.

Sources indicate that L-BAIBA has attracted scientific interest for more than a decade. In research published in 2014, Roberts demonstrated that the molecule has beneficial effects on metabolism, helping to enhance the body's ability to burn fat in response to exercise. L-BAIBA is now commercially available as a dietary supplement.

In a recent development, the latest findings reveal another important function of the molecule. L-BAIBA acts as a chemical messenger that connects physical activity with beneficial changes in muscle structure and metabolism, helping muscles adapt to the demands placed on them.

Lee Roberts, Professor of Molecular Physiology and Metabolism at the University of Leeds, noted: "Our research identifies L-BAIBA as an exercise-induced signal that helps muscles adapt, improve their metabolic capacity and ability to contract, and ultimately enhances physical performance.

"This gives us exciting latest insight into how exercise benefits the body and highlights a promising target for future therapies aimed at preserving muscle function in chronic conditions such as diabetes.".

Protecting Muscles Against Damage From Type 2 Diabetes.

It has been revealed that the researchers also discovered that L-BAIBA protects muscles against damage associated with type 2 diabetes. The condition can negatively affect muscle health, leading to a decline in muscle mass and strength, as well as disruptions in the way muscles process and use energy. These complications can significantly reduce a person's quality of life.

Because regular physical activity is an notable part of managing type 2 diabetes, finding ways to improve muscle function and reduce fatigue could make a substantial difference for people who struggle to exercise.

In a recent development, type 2 diabetes is a serious chronic condition that increases the risk of potentially life-threatening complications, including heart attacks and strokes. Its development is influenced by a complex combination of factors, including age, ethnicity, genetics, and living with overweight or obesity.

Although type 2 diabetes has traditionally been more common among older adults, diagnoses in people younger than 40 have been rising in recent years. Cases in this younger age group are now increasing more rapidly than among adults over 40.

A Promising Target for Future Diabetes Treatments.

Anna Morris, Assistant Director of Research Strategy and Partnership at Diabetes UK, noted: "Exercise plays an important role in managing type 2 diabetes, but for many people muscle weakness and fatigue can make staying active a real challenge. This research helps us better understand how muscles adapt to exercise and identifies a potential latest target for improving muscle health. While these findings are still at an early stage, they could help shape future approaches that support people with type 2 diabetes to remain active and live healthier, longer lives.".

Although the discovery opens promising avenues for future treatments, further research is needed to determine whether L-BAIBA supplementation can produce meaningful therapeutic benefits in people with type 2 diabetes.

The study was funded by Diabetes UK and BBSRC.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 is a technical marvel, one that's left a veteran game artist with credits on The Last of Us Part 2 Remastered and Star Wars Jedi: Survivor so stunned, he indicates he "didn't know this was possible.".

Industry observers note that del Walker is a lead character artist at Absurd Ventures who previously worked at Naughty Dog and Respawn Entertainment, and he's been giving his overwhelmingly positive thoughts on GTA 6 to Bloomberg reporter Jason Schreier (below). Referring specifically to the game's graphics, he notes: "Everything they're doing is what we have been told never to do in every game I've been on.".

For example, Schreier explains that during his conversation with the dev, Walker pointed to the fact that you normally only see a few characters on screen at any point with realistic hair that actually moves strand by strand, with NPCs usually made in a modular way that makes them look generic. This sort of thing comes in an effort to achieve reasonable scope and 60fps, Schreier notes.

It has been revealed that obviously, though, not only did Rockstar opt for a 30fps target on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, but the devs went above and beyond with the detail of their NPCs, with them being individually art directed and given their own personality traits to boot. As Walker puts it, "It's like looking at a skyscraper, but I'm from the 1800s. I didn't know this was possible.".

Sources indicate that he's not the only one impressed, of course. One game designer on The Last of Us Part 2 has called GTA 6 "the Great Pyramids of Game Development," saying that "people will be asking for centuries how it was possible and we will eventually conclude that aliens made it.".

It's for good reason, of course. Even with such a lengthy development cycle and a clearly immense budget (that Rockstar won't confirm beyond saying it's not $1.5 billion), GTA 6 really is a sight to behold – there's no wonder that other devs are contemplating the sorcery behind it. As Walker so eloquently puts it, "I don't know shit about fuck. Rockstar do, clearly.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After a couple of delays, a plagiarism lawsuit, and at least one internal reboot, Bungie’s next big game has officially rolled out. Marathon, the extraction shooter from the studio behind Destiny, has managed to find a decent, if a little small of an audience.

The game’s player numbers on Steam are being compared to its recent free, open weekend, and not in a favourable manner.

Prior to Marathon’s launch, Bungie held a multi-day Server Slam, which offered anyone interested in playing the game a chance to try out almost all of its classes, two of its maps, as well as many of its gameplay and progression systems.

The open test was largely well-received, and players actually highlighted up for it. It peaked at a very respectable 143,621 concurrent players on Steam, which put it within striking distance of the peak concurrent of its chief competitor, Arc Raiders - at least when you compare both of their pre-launch Server Slam events.

Industry observers note that in Arc Raiders’ case, those figures were far outpaced at the game’s actual launch, and the Embark shooter continues to command a very active player base to this day. A paid product garnering far more players than the same product’s own free sampler is never not a good sign, so many hoped something similar would happen with Marathon.

Recent findings suggest that marathon has now officially debuted, and it doesn’t look like it managed to pull an Arc Raiders - at least so far. At its peak, the Bungie shooter attracted 88,337 concurrent players on Steam (via SteamDB), which is a little over half of its Server Slam’s 143,621 peak concurrent.

Numbers have, of course, dropped since then, which is normal, as players log off for the night. This is obviously not the end of the road for Marathon. Friday, and the weekend, may well push numbers closer to the Server Slam heights.

It has been revealed that indeed, word of mouth is quite positive, with the game currently sitting at a Very Positive user review rating on Steam, based on over 4,600 reviews. As has been proven time and time again in recent years, nothing catapults a game like players emphatically advocating for it to their friends, so it could simply be that mainstream players are cautious.

It will become clear where things settle over the weekend.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The difference is that you're doing this inside a huge walking fortress city, which stamps across the surface of a largely unseen, devastated and uninhabitable Earth.
  • It has been revealed that from a certain, carefully limited point of view, this transforms Steel Gullet into the kind of "Zen experience" I hope death-positive morticians have when really absorbed in their work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it's amazing what a difference a few lines of preamble can make to your understanding of a game. Out now on PC, Steel Gullet is a factory engineering puzzler that, while notable for its meticulous interest in thermodynamics, broadly compares to the foundational work of Zachtronics, together with more recent and focussed conveyor belt wranglers such as Modulus. Resources come in, and you arrange machines on a grid to transform them into something else, before sliding them into an output hopper.

The difference is that you're doing this inside a huge walking fortress city, which stamps across the surface of a largely unseen, devastated and uninhabitable Earth. Your resources are the refuse of a bygone human civilisation: knots of concrete and rebar, flaccid rubber hose and splintered plank, that must be separated out before you can manufacture anything.

It has been revealed that from a certain, carefully limited point of view, this transforms Steel Gullet into the kind of "Zen experience" I hope death-positive morticians have when really absorbed in their work. My task is to lay a civilisation to rest, by dissecting and cleansing the remains, readying a fallen objectworld for an after-life that extends somewhere beyond the map's huge rusty walls (walls that, perhaps appropriately, constrain your camera movement a bit too much for comfort).

In a recent development, it makes me think of the vertigo I get when I look at devices such as, well, the computer I'm writing this on, and think about how many materials and histories of production lie entangled within it. Steel Gullet answers the desire for clarity and accounting there. Of course, the other part of the premise is that I am doing busywork for some kind of totalitarian organisation, G.R.I.D. But shh, no time to think about that! I'm trying to work out how hot rubber needs to be before it can be moulded.

Thermodynamics is Steel Gullet's fixation, and a worthwhile one. Every material encased in each lump of salvage has different physical properties – a melting point, density, solubility, ferromagnetism, etcetera. You meed to exploit these differences to separate the pieces. Wood, for example, is more buoyant than metal and concrete, so if you feed the clump into an oil bath, the planks will float to the top. If there's rubber, you can run the clump through furnaces to melt and drain it, then cool and reheat the resulting puddle to create a malleable material.

According to recent reports, it's still just the usual automation game routine of funnelling greebly wotsits through various smashy boxes to produce a commodity. But the thermodynamics sim element both supports the above feeling of purifying a hopelessly muddled world, and makes for a surprising visual feast: I enjoy watching each material emerge from the inital jumble and assume different shapes. There are the usual supporting infrastructure elements, such as elevators, splitters and manual junction boxes. I dare say somebody will build a logic circuit in Steel Gullet, sooner or later - let's start the clock till they get Doom running on the thing.

In terms of overall strategy, you alternate between sending outputs to hoppers that earn you cash, and sending them to hoppers that generate research progression. You'll also unlock latest rooms, removing walls and exposing new output hoppers. As you're issued new work orders, you must break open your production lines to install new machines and redirect the flow. Fortunately, you can sell back components to keep your cash reserves healthy – or at least, you can in the demo.

Sources indicate that between chapters, you'll be invited to join the resistance against the aforesaid G.R.I.D., perhaps sending information to the rebels. But again, no time, no time! I have all this concrete I need to powderise, all these girders I need to liquefy and make upcoming, all these crisp, gleaming circuitboards I need to manufacture. The city's hunger is as vast as it is holy. Read more on Steam.

Sources indicate that britain's Marc 'Caedrel' Lamont and Dan Gaskin were among the winners at the 2026 Esports Awards in Miami, where Counter-Strike 2 was named game of the year and Team Vitality and BLAST also took industry honours. The results crown a strong Counter-Strike year eight days before the next CS2 Major begins in Singapore.

It has been revealed that the 2026 Esports Awards honoured two British figures from the streaming and broadcast side of the scene. Caedrel is a League of Legends streamer and co-streamer. Gaskin works as a caster.

The ceremony took place on the evening of 17 November at the Adrienne Arsht Center for the Performing Arts of Miami-Dade County. It is the scene’s main end-of-season awards show. The event began in London in 2016.

At Worlds 2026, Caedrel was the top co-streamer for both hours watched and peak viewers, according to Esports Charts.

Sources indicate that his co-stream success came in a softer year for the tournament overall. Worlds 2026 peaked at 3.98 million viewers, which was 41% lower than the previous year. Caedrel’s numbers show how much attention a single co-streamer can hold even when the event’s headline peak falls.

Recent findings suggest that gaskin was not the only caster honoured in Miami. The other broadcast honours went to Alex ‘Machine’ Richardson for Play-by-Play Caster of the Year, Iain Chambers for Host of the Year and Anthony ‘NAMELESS’ Wheeler for Analyst of the Year. iShowSpeed was named Streamer of the Year.

In a recent development, counter-Strike featured prominently among the industry prizes. Vitality’s award as best organisation came alongside Esports PC Player of the Year for Mathieu ‘ZywOo’ Herbaut. OpTic Texas were named Esports Team of the Year.

BLAST, which stages many of its events in Europe, was named Esports Tournament Organiser of the Year.

Sources indicate that vitality’s results through the year back up their award. They beat Spirit to win IEM Rio 2026 on 19 April, giving them back-to-back ESL Grand Slam titles. ZywOo took his 31st career HLTV MVP award at that event.

"When I won this award in 2023, I never thanked my parents" 😅❤️.

Esports Colour Caster of the Year — @DanGaskin pic.twitter.com/oZBw5FItEJ.

— Esports Awards Presented by Thunderpick (@esportsawards) November 18, 2026.

It has been revealed that the team’s form held into the autumn. Vitality swept MOUZ 3-0 in the ESL Pro League Season 24 grand final on 11 October. That was their second title in a row after winning StarSeries Fall in September.

The PGL Major Singapore 2026 runs from 25 November to 13 December with 32 teams and a US$1,250,000 prize pool, The Kallang reported. The final stages will be played at the Singapore Indoor Stadium from 10 to 13 December.
